Sir WILFRID LAURIER moved that the House -will, to-morrow move itself into Committee of the Whole House to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to authorize the Governor in Council to, on or after the seventh of April, 1911, grant a subsidy for steamship service between a port or ports on the Pacific coast of Canada and China and Japan, for such period or periods of time as may be deemed expedient, not, however, to exceed in the aggregate ten years, and to pay therefor a subsidy or subsidies, as the case may be, not exceeding the sum of 25,000 pounds sterling per annum for such service as may be deemed expedient from time to time.
He said:	His Excellency having been
advised of the subject matter of this resolution recommends it to the favourable consideration of this House.
Motion agreed to.

I desire to ask the government to what extent the International regu-Mr. KING.
lations for the protection of fisheries in the Great Lakes and other international waters have been modified. On this point the Detroit ' Free Press ' of Friday, January
13, says:

maintopic: MICHIGAN WILL GAIN BIG ADVANTAGES FROM PROVISIONS OF TREATY.

speechtext:
Special to the Free Press.
Washington, January 12.-It is reasonably certain now that the treaty between the United States and Canada covering the fisheries question on the Great Lakes will, before its promulgation, be satisfactory in every respect to the fishermen of the state of Michigan.
It can be stated that not only will Lake Michigan be exempted from the regulations to be promulgated in the treaty, but that practically half of Lake Huron will be given over to the fishermen of Michigan for their operations. In other words, they will be allowed to operate from a point east of Thunder Bay to a point south near Port Sanilac in Lake Huron. This will give them everything they desire. The new proposition will be added to the fishing regulations as an amendment.
It is also proposed that the Michigan fishing regulations shall be adopted by the international commission, and to-day Senator Smith wired Governor Osborn to send at once a copy of the state fishing laws to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries of Canada.
I would ask the Prime Minister whether the statements contained in this dispatch are correct and also whether any action was taken by this government to investigate the conditions which exist among the fishermen on the Canadian side of the Detroit river, and if it is probable that the Detroit river will be exempted from the provisions of the proposed treaty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: MICHIGAN WILL GAIN BIG ADVANTAGES FROM PROVISIONS OF TREATY.
speechtext: With regard to the question whether the government has investigated the condition of things prevailing in the Detroit river, I have no information ; perhaps the Minister of Marine has. The treaty is before the House, but no modification has been agreed to yet. Whether any is contemplated or not I do not know.

I would like to ask the Prime Minister for an answer to my question of Friday last regarding a mail car to Cochrane. I see that we have back with us the Postmaster General, and I trust this matter has been brought to his attention.
The report made at the request of the Prime Minister was brought before me this morning, and I may say that I signed the report, and the postal car will be there next week.

The Prime Minister promised a statement to-day with

regard to the recent negotiations incident to the award of the Hague Tribunal.

I would like to ask the right hon. the Prime Minister it the proposed reciprocity treaty will be submitted to this House for consideration before it is signed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think the treaty will be submitted to the House before it is signed, but it will not go into force until it is ratified by this parliament.

If the treaty is to be signed before it is submitted to the House for consideration then I wish to give notice that I intend to move a resolution to the effect that treaties of commerce, before they are signed or ratified, should be laid before this parliament for consideration for a certain length of time.

I would like to call the attention of the right hon. the First Minister to some orders for returns which I would like to have as soon as possible. I would like to ask the Minister of Labour if the government will be responsible for the whole or any part of the remuneration to be paid to Judge Barron who is investigating the claims of the recent strikers on the Grand Trunk.
No.

I would like to inquire of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries when I may expect a return, the order for which passed the House last year, with reference to the fines imposed and the names of the persons fined for breach of the fishery regulations in the counties of Cumberland and Pictou. Three or four weeks ago the hon. minister informed me that the returns had been prepared and had been handed to the Secretary of -State. Within the past two days I have inquired of the Secretary of State, and he has informed me that he has seen no such return. I also inquired of the Under Secretary of State, and he says the same thing. I hope the minister will see that the return is brought down immediately.

Mr. Speaker, I intend, in connection- with this motion, to bring before the House and the country the claim of the Canadian people who use the Canadian Pacific railway for a reduction in the tariff of that railway, and I propose to approach it in this way :
That before the said motion do pass, this House hereby declares that steps should be at once taken to ascertain the rights of the public using the Canadian Pacific railway to a reduced tariff because of provision in that regard contained in the Act of parliament ratifying the agreement with that company, or any other Act.
I have added the words, ' or any other Act,' as I wanted to make it clear that I was cognizant of what is said to be the fact, t-hat the railway company now admits that it is under the operation of the General Railway Act, and I intend to approach this question in an absolutely impartial and non-partisan way. I hope to approach it as speaking for all the people of Canada who use that great railway, a railway that has now over 10,000 miles of track in operation, which serves every province in Canada with the single exception of the little island of Prince Edward. I hope I shall speak for the people of the east, the manufacturers of Ontario and the people of Ontario, for those who live on and, cultivate the plains, and for the people of the Pacific coast, who also use the railroad. I admit that it is a great railway ; it is a magnificent railway ; it is the greatest triumph, the greatest memorial, Sir John Macdonald left after him. The Canadian

Pacific railway is an immense success. Of all the things in Canadian history that had hirth in this House, it is the one that has vindicated itself. Perhaps it is greater than the National Policy. As it set out in tlie preamble, it was the Canadian Pacific railway that bound this country together. It was built for a great national reason, and it is to the credit of those men who sat in this House in the early days and propounded that policy, carried it out, vindicated it, and at last saw it triumph, and also saw those who opposed it at its inception come to justify it, to be proud of it, and to be active in its defence. But if I admit the greatness of that railroad and the service it renders, I am not blind to the duties that its charter imposed. With all great public franchises great duties go-	.
There is a duty involved. There are public rights as well as the rights of the company to be considered, and to-day I am raising my voice on behalf of those public rights which the people have in the original charter and subsequent laws to a reduction in the charges imposed by that railway-whether those charges be for fares, for sleepers, or parlour cars, or for meals in dining or refreshment rooms, or freights, for express, telegraph or telephone charges, for electricity, if it be sold, and for even water charges in connection with steamers that may form a part of its railway system; so that while I admire the greatness of the Canadian Pacific railway and its success and what it has done to build up the credit of Canada, I also raise my voice in the matter of the duties which that road owes to this country-duties in the way of service and most of all its duty to have its rates revised in the interests of the people who pay them. I hope to be able to show that the time has come when parliament or some body must interfere so as to secure a reduction in these rates.
Just for a moment I want to read the clause in the original Act which deals with the rates of the company and which, I am told, if not obsolete or repealed, is to-day ineffective. Whether that be so or not, it certainly throws a lot of light on the matter. I propose to read, in the first place, clause 20 of the Statutes of Canada, 1881, chapter 1. That clause reads as follows:-
The limit to the reduction of tolls by the parliament of Canada provided for by the eleventh subsection of the 17th section of The Consolidated Railway Act of 1879, respecting tolls, is hereby extended so that such reduction may be to such an extent that such tolls when reduced shall not produce less than 10 per cent per annum profit on the capital actually expended in the construction of the railway, instead of not less than 15 per cent per annum profit as provided by the said subsection; and so also that such reduction shall not be made unless the net income of the company, ascertained as described in said Mr. MACLEAN.
subsection, shall have exceeded 10 per cent per annum instead of 15 per cent per annum as provided by the said subsection, and the exercise by the Governor in Council of the power of reducing the tolls of the company as provided by the 10th subsection of said section 17 is hereby limited to the same extent with relation to the profit of the company and to its net revenue, as that to which the power of parliament to reduce tolls is limited by said subsection 11 as hereby amended.
That is rather complicated and tough, reading, but you get a little elucidation if you read the Railway Act, which is quoted in that section. That Railway Act was passed in 1879, two years before the Canadian Pacific railway charter was granted, and its clauses are 10, 11 and 12:-
10.	Every by-law fixing and regulating tolls shall be subject to revision by the Governor in Council from time to time after approval thereof, and after an order in council, reducing the tolls fixed and regulated by any by-law, has been twice published in the 'Canada Gazette/ the tolls mentioned in such an order in council shall be substituted for those mentioned in said by-law so long as the order in council remains unrevoked.
11.	The parliament of Canada may from time to time reduce the tolls upon the railway, but not without consent of the company, or so as to produce less than 15 per cent per annum profit on the capital actually expended in its construction, nor unless on an examination made by the Minister of Public Works of the amount received and expended by the company, the net income from all sources for the year then last passed is found to have exceeded 15 per cent upon the capital so actually expended.
12.	No by-law of any railway company by which any tolls are to be imposed or altered, or by which any party other than the members, officers and servants of the company are intended to be bound, shall have any force or effect until the same has been approved and sanctioned by the Governor in Council.
In substance, those two laws amount to-this: Under the general law, a railway could have its tolls reduced if the net profit from its operation exceeded 15 per cent of the amount actually expended in its construction, but in the case of the Canadian Pacific railway the government or parliament, or some one, was to have power to reduce the tolls whenever the net income of the road exceeded 10 per cent of the amount of money actually invested in it. In other words, the people were to be treated under the Canadian Pacific Railway Act 5 per cent better than under the general Act. That was in substance the arrangement; apparently some means should have been taken by the Canadian Pacific railway or the government of the day to have an account kept of the money actually expended on construction. Evidently, however, nothing of that kind was done, and1

the thins dragged along and no question was raised and no one knew exactly how matters stood.
One reason why the Canadian Pacific railway was asked to treat the public so much better was because it was given exceptional advantages. It was given $25,-O00,000 in cash, 25,000,000 acres of land, customs exemptions, exemptions from the municipal law, rival lines were prohibited, and in many other ways had special privileges and powers conferred on it.
But in connection with all these advantages, there was a clause to this effect, that inasmuch as the railway was getting all these things it should do something for the public in return, and consequently there was a provision guaranteeing to the government control of the rates. The essence of the agreement was whenever a certain thing happened the public were entitled to a reduction in the tolls. That matter was brought up and discussed in this House many times by myself and by members from the west' and other portions of the country, but always some special pleading was raised to prevent this clause from taking effect. One by one, however, the special privileges pleaded on behalf of the Canadian Pacific railway have been removed-some by the payment of money and others by other means. When the Crows-nest Pass charter was granted, it was granted on the condition that the Canadian Pacific railway should reduce its rates in the west. Then the prohibition against rival roads was removed at the instance of the people of Manitoba. So in various ways special privileges disappeared, and only one remains, the exemption from taxes, which is now, I believe, before the Privv Council.
Whenever these questions were brought up, we never could get a satisfactory answer We were always treated to evasions and were told that they have to be settled by the courts. The last statement ever made in this connection was that 'made by the then Minister of Justice, now Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, who acknowledged, to me that the company had abandoned its claim to the protection of the 10 per cent clause in the original charter and admitted that it came under the jurisdiction of the Railway Act and the Board of Railway Commissioners. And, to show that that is the situation today, I propose to quote a statement by Mr. Creelman, the counsel of the Canadian Pacific which appeared in a Toronto newspaper the other day. This is a despatch, dated Montreal, January 10, and I wish to Tead it because it is the first written or printed document that I have seen which states the abandonment by the Canadian Pacific railway of any protection in this Tespect that it enjoyed under the original charter. We have had the statement of the
former Minister of Justice, and I have seen statements in the newspapers, that the company would submit itself to the Railway Commission, but this statement by Mr. Creelman is the first I have seen from that source, and I propose to read it in order to get it on the records:-
In an interview to-night Mr. A. R. Creelman, K.C., general counsel for the Canadian Pacific railway, and also one of the directors of the company, discussed the recent increase in dividend of the company.
' Will the increase in the dividend to ten per cent mean that the company must submit its rates to the Railway Commission? ' Mr. Creelman was asked.
' Not at all/ was his answer. ' The declaration of an extra dividend was made in view of the position of the land account, and of the other extraneous assets of the company. The distribution from these sources, commencing with the payment of the next quarterly dividend, will be at the rate of three per cent per annum, instead of one per cent as heretofore/	, .
' Does not your charter call for a revision of rates by the government as soon as your company pays ten per cent ? '
' No, such is not the case/ was his reply.
' Our charter says that neither parliament nor the Governor General in Council shall reduce our rates until the railway is making ten per cent net on the actual capital expended in the construction of the road/
' And what is the amount expended in actual construction?'
' We do not know/ said Mr. Creelman.
' Some time ago we took up this matter with the Supreme Court in order to have them determine what the actual expenditure was. We wanted to know whether it meant only the main line, or whether it included branches, terminals, &c. That case is still pending, but, as a matter of fact, the Canadian Pacific railway agreed some years ago not to claim) the protection of the ten per cent clause, and, further, we have repeatedly expressed our willingness to submit our rates to the Railway Commission to have them deal with them on their merits. In other words, in so far as our rates aup concerned, we have been in the same position as any other railway in Canada. We have voluntarily submitted our rates to the Railway Commission whenever these rates have been attacked.
' And, after all/ he added, ' rates are determined by the business of the country and by competition. We could not arbitrarily fix rates which would he excessive.' ' There has been/ said Mr. Creelman, ' a good deal of misunderstanding regarding this ten per cent clause. But it only refers to a time when the road is making ten per cent net on the actual capital expended on construction. And, further, we have never taken refuge behind our rates agreement, but have freely submitted our rates to the Railway Commission. So far as our rates are concerned, we have been in the same position as other roads in Canada.
Now, as I read it, that practically means that the Canadian Pacific railway came before the Board of Railway Commissioners,

and admitted that they were under that jurisdiction and would so remain. If that is so, it is very important that we should know it; it is very important that a matter of such great concern to the people of Canada should be definitely stated.
Was it not stated in this House two years ago ?

adian Pacific has indulged in in the past. Mr. Creelman goes on to speak of referring rates to the Railway Commission ' to have them deal with them on their merits.' I hope they will be dealt with on their merits, and it is with that view that I bring the matter up to-day. He speaks of ' whenever these rates have been attacked.' Apparently, he is ready to -meet the attack, if such it be, when made before the Railway Commission; and, in substance, my proposal this afternoon is to make that attack on his rates before the Railway Commission and to have the parliament of Canada order it to be done in such a way that the public shall have relief. I have heard another rumour, and I believe there is a good deal of truth in it, that the Canadian Pacific railway is prepared to come down in its rates the moment it is asked to do so. And there are reasons why its rates should come down.
Before I take that up, I want to deal for a moment with this so-called settlement that took place. Why did the coon come down? The coon came down, apparently, from the Governor in Council revising the rates. The coon came down, and something else also happened. Perhaps Mr. Davy Crockett put down his gun when he went for the coon. Anyway, some kind of an investigation was held; I have been told that something took place in the Supreme Court. Will the Minister of Railways help me by saying whether that was the case? Was this matter of the control of rates referred to the Supreme Court?
A case was prepared for submission to the Supreme Court, but it was never carried out.

Then counsel must have been employed. If a case was prepared, then counsel was employed by the government. There was a Davy Crockett, there was a gun, and there was a coon, and the coon came down. There was a case, and the jurisdiction simply was changed. The people were complaining of the high rates. Somebody must have had a grievance. But after they proceeded under the special Act they said: The coon says it is a hard thing to find out under the special Act, and we will do it in the Railway Commission, and under the General Railway Act. So the coon came down, and counsel was dismissed, apparently there was no more appeal to the Supreme Court, and there the matter rested. Why did counsel abandon that case in the Supreme Court under the special Act, instead of forthwith pursuing it under the general Act, and under the same instructions? Now, that is a matter that ought to be explained, and I hope the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Justice will explain it here to-day.

Because it looked as if the people were going to get their rights, that the railway was afraid to go to court and to tell how much the road was costing, what had happened to all the things it had got. To-day the Canadian Pacific railway would not like to go into court and say what they did with the twenty-five millions of stock they had got a right to issue, and whether any money was obtained from that, and whether it went into the undertaking. They might not like to have their accounts opened up in regard to contracts, in regard to what the road actually cost. Although it was a hard undertaking for them, and they had great trouble in financing it, the original figures might show that it cost a comparatively small amount. Anyway, when they were afraid of that issue, and when the people apparently had a grievance as to the regulation of freights, the proceedings stopped, and from that day to this anybody who has had a grievance in connection with that railway must be satisfied to proceed under the general Act governing railways.
Now, I would still like to know from the minister who the counsel vras that was employed, what was the case he had worked up, why they left the Supreme Court with the matter, and why it is, when an arrangement was reached that redress was to be handed out by the Board of Railway Commissioners, no further steps were taken to remedy the grievances of the people of the Canadian west, and of the Canadian east, against the Canadian Pacific railway. That there were grievances, the walls of this House know well. They have resounded with the cry of the people of the west, and even of the people of the east, for an amelioriation of the traffic charges of that great company, and that complaint still continues. I hardly ever take up a Toronto paper that I do not read that the Board of Trade, or the merchants there have a substantial grievance against the Canadian Pacific railway. I read about the Board of Trade in Winnipeg almost every week expressing a grievance against the traffic charges of the Canadian Pacific railway. There was a deputation of farmers down here not long ago and they filed in this chamber, at an interview with the Prime Minister and some of his colleagues, a document setting forth their grievance against the railways. I will now read from the * Grain Growers' Guide ' of December 28, on page 12, a sentence from a paper presented by Mr. James Bower, president of the United Farmers of Alberta:
Tlie third question to which we would refer you is the excessive railway tolls, both passenger and freight, which are burdens keenly felt by the farmers all over Canada.
Now, I reiterate that statement in connection with the Canadian Pacific railway;
their rates are excessive. I will put one other witness in the box, and that is Mr. Charles Melville Hays, president of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, and general manager, and probably president, of the Grand Trunk railway. Not long ago he had a strike on his railway of the trainmen. They came to him with their grievance, and he said to them: I cannot very well increase your pay just now, I cannot give you as much as you ask, because the Grand Trunk is not yet doing business in the Canadian west where railway rates are high and profitable. New, Mr. Hays, president of the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific, made the confession that in his estimation the charges taken by the Canadian Pacific railway from the public of the west were very profitable, and he regretted that he was not a participant therein. Now, there is a further witness as to these excessive tolls, which are a burden keenly felt by the farmers all over Canada. In Ontario, in the maritime provinces, in the west, on the Pacific coast, they are excessive, and the time has come for them to be reduced. But as I say, I have another witness. Somebody has been pursuing the Canadian Pacific railway before the Railway Commission to-day, in the matter of excessive express charges, and I ask the Minister of Railways who instituted that action.
I understand that is the Dominion Express Company.
Understanding that, will he please answer the question: Who instituted it? Was it under the direction of the government?

If I remember rightly, the investigation began on a special complaint from certain sections of the people as to the rates, and as the inquiry involved large questions, it was made a general investigation.
Under instructions from the government?
The investigation was made general because the special case could not be investigated without going into the whole case. That is my understanding of it.

There is a confession from the Minister of Railways that the express rates were excessive, and he went for the express companies and I give him credit for it. He should have gone after them in respect to passenger rates, telegraph rates, telephone rates, sleeping car rates. [DOT] The case is made out. The farmers spoke of the excessive rates which are a burden on the public, and that is proved by the fact that the government themsel-

ves have undertaken to instruct counsel to have the express charges modified. What did the commission find? I am going to read from the Montreal ' Witness I shall not read the first two lines which compliment myself, and that would not do.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.
Read.
Oh, no.
I will read them when it comes to my turn.

Among other things, shortly discuss the extension of the .parcels post, is again remindful that while Great Britain has for many years had a parcel post service in connection with the post office which is efficient and cheap in a high degree, the United States and Canada have been so under the thumb of the express companies that the government of neither country has been able to throw off their yoke, and their yoke is heavy indeed.
In Canada we have recently had a report from the Railway Commission on express charges, and they were found to be so profitable as to open the eyes of the public very wide. The commissioners told us that the Canadian Express Company in conjunction with the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and the Dominion Express Company in conjunction with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, have been taking out of the pockets of the people something like 55 and 65 per cent profits respectively on excessively watered stocks. The commissioners call attention to other queer doings, and orders them, among other orders, to reduce their charges by ten per cent.
And the correspondent wTho had read that wants to know why they did not make them reduce the tariff 40 per cent.
Here is another proof of what the farmers buffer from excessive railway charges in Canada, including those of the Canadian Pacific railway. So excessive are they that the government has been forced-or let us say rather has, as a matter of public policy, intervened and put counsel to work, and so successfully that the Railway Commission has been convinced of the wrongdoing that was uncovered and a reduction of tolls has been ordered. Now, we have the fruit growers expressing some appreciation of this Act of the government and the hope that its effects will be extended. Is there any other proof of the excessive charges of this railway? I am going to leave it to the members of this House who represent various constituencies throughout the country to state whether these charges are excessive. Let the men- who represent the west, let the men who represent British Columbia, tell us whether they like the treatment they are getting from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

British Columbia has ports of her own upon the Pacific ocean, freight comes around the Horn and up to Victoria and Vancouver, is unloaded there,- and what sort of charges do the Canadian Pacific railway impose upon that freight for a hundred miles inland? Are the people of British Columbia satisfied with that treatment? It takes nearly as much to send that freight inland for a hundred miles or two hundred miles from the Pacific coast, as if it were landed at Montreal and sent westward by train. They have a great grievance in the west. So have the farmers of the plains, so have the manufacturers of Ontario, so have the people of the east. They are all complaining of these excessive freight charges, the case has been fully established and the time has come for some kind of revision of these rates.
If I may change my course a bit, I want to take another view of this issue, and it is this: Can the Canadian Pacific Railway Company stand a revision of its rates? What shape is its treasury in? In what position is it, to use the language of the original Act, to stand reductions- that is the word in the original Act-in its tolls where there is an excessive profit? Is there an excessive profit and cannot it stand a reduction in its tolls? That is a matter which will be really easy to reach. There never was such a fat treasury in anything in connection with the history of Canada as the treasury of the Canadian Pacific railway to-day. For proof of that let me quote that good old newspaper, the Toronto ' Globe.' Last week it had an article on ' The Year of Jubilee.' Oh, you people in the west, the year of jubilee has arrived for you, according to the ' Globe,' and here it is:-
The burghers of Amsterdam

Happy burghers.
-who many years ago bought Canadian Pacific railway stock because a man named Van Horne was at the head of the company must have rejoiced greatly yesterday when they learned that they would hereafter get a dividend of ten per cent on stock they bought twenty years ago for about forty cents on the dollar. Thousands of Canadians who have had faith in the Canadian Pacific railway and have from time to time acquired Canadian Pacific railway stocks had great reason to rejoice also. This is a year of jubilee for the shareholders of the great railway.
What about the poor devil raising wheat out at Pile-o'-Bones and the . freight charges he has to pay? Is it a year of jubilee for him? Does the ' Globe ' give him any consideration now? Where is the year of jubilee for him? Are there not excessive freight charges that he has to pay? Of course, a line or two down, the ' Globe ' says that it is going to be a year

of jubilee for him, and the Canadian Pacific railway hereafter is going to get along without rate regulation, and that the residents of the west are also to participate in it, but they want to participate in it in the same way and they say: If your shareholders gets large dividends we should have reduced tolls. We see that the ten per cent dividend has arrived, we see the year of jubilee for the Dutch, the foreign owners of the road, but what about the native Canadian who pays the tolls? I am speaking to-day for the native Canadian or any resident of this country who has to pay tolls on that great railway. What else have we got, besides this year of jubilee, which the ' Globe ' is so glad has arrived for the Dutch shareholder?
I think that Sir William Van Horne is about the greatest man who ever came to this country. He has made a glorious name for himself in Canada.
What rate do they actually earn on their capital?

I am coming to that in a moment. I think Sir William Van Horne is one of our greatest men and that he has done this country a splendid service, but I would have wished that when his monument came to be raised the inscription on it would be twofold-that he did well for his shareholders but he did better for the people who had to pay the railway rates of this country. I met a man the other day who is performing a great public service at the present moment, and he said to me: I am discharging that public service in this country and I hope to get some of the flowers handed to me before they put them on my grave; the flowers I want handed to me now are the appreciation of the public service I am doing. That man is engaged in the operation of a great public franchise owned by the public, and that is his idea of appreciation in that respect.
But, we do not require even to take the ' Globe ' for the story of the year of jubilee. Here is the finest document that I have read for a long while. I get a copy of this every year, so does every hon. member of this House. I think it is in the charter and I will give the Canadian Pacific railway credit for discharging that part of the duties imposed upon it* namely, giving a copy of. its annual report to every member of this House. It is a document that is remarkable for what it contains, what it does not contain, and what you can dig out of it if you have the spade and the method. It is a document that would never pass muster before the Interstate Commerce Commission of the United States. They have changed all that now and every statement presented to the Interstate Commerce Commission
must be much more detailed and much more exact as to the thing that it pur-., ports to tell. I am going to read just a few statements in this report and comment on them:

29th Annual Report of the Directors, Year Ended June 30.
The accounts of the company for the year ended June 30, 1910, show the following results :-
I wish gentlemen who have this report would follow the figures. On the first page of this statement of the accounts of the company it says that they actually get in interest on deposits and loans $904,000 a year. It is a pretty good company that receives such an amount in interest. Then it gets a million and a half additional on dividends on certain stocks which it owns. In other words, from these two sources it gets $2,500,000 every year. Its net earnings last year wrere $34,000,000, nearly a million a week, after paying all its running expenses, and its net surplus is $13,-
500,000.	The average price at which it sold its land was over $14 an acre. Little statements occur in other paragraphs of the report which are illuminative. For instance, it says:-
You will be asked to authorize the issue and sale of a sufficient amount of 4 per cent consolidated debenture stock to provide for the construction of the following branch lines.
Then it enumerates an enormous number of branch lines to be built with 4 per cent debenture stock. The next paragraph states that another railroad is to be acquired at a rental equivalent to the interest at 4 per cent per annum on the bonds of the railway, and still another railway is to be acquired on similar terms. When they acquire other railroads it is by paying 4 per cent on bonds, the proceeds of which were actually spent in construction.
I go from the report to the condensed balance sheet to June 30. There is a statement of assets and liabilities, and will defy anybody, even the best chartered accountant in America or Canada, to tell me by that statement what the actual assets of the company are. It is marvellous for not showing what the assets of that great company to-day are. That is the significant deduction to be made from the statement. It says that the railway and equipment is worth $317,000,000, and I thought that probably that was all that had been put into the report in that way, but I saw at page 17 just a little note at the bottom dealing with the whole history of the land fund. nIt says:-
Amount expended in construction of railway and equipment and deducted from cost of property, $36,000,000.

That is, the Canadian Pacific railway has applied to construction and equipment out of its land fund already $36,000,000. Thus, we must add to the value of the railway and equipment as given, that is $317,000,000, this further sum of $36,000,000 that had been applied to it from the land fund. How could that, then, be a statement of its assets or its value, when that amount has been carefully deducted?
Then they give a list of acquired securities, the most magnificent list of acquired securities I have seen in a long time. They are all put down at their cost, and I suppose that there, or in*the next item, you would find, some place, if you could dig down, the acquired securities in connection with the Dominion Express Company, up in the millions, according to the Railway Commission, but not stated here at all. That is all watered stock, apparently, and I suppose it is only put down as a few thousand dollars.
. Then this company has this magnificent item of current assets, amounting to $6,-
900,000,	and it has $46,000,000 in cash in its treasury. It has something else, it has temporarily invested in government securities ten million dollars and over. So great is the Canadian Pacific railway to-dav that it is the banker for the government of Canada. Forty-six millions in its treasury. $10,000,000 additional temporarily invested in government securities, and which I believe was money really loaned to the government of this country. That is the condition of the treasury of this great company.
Thus, besides all its railroads and other things, it has assets a good deal over $100,000,000, that ought, in my contention, to be applied to a reduction of rates. I do not see why a great railway, great as it may be, should be allowed to accumulate an enormous reserve fund like that and be a banker for the country in which it is located and be temporarily investing in government securities. From a banker's point of view, it does not pay to give shareholders 10 per cent on stock and to get that money in the treasury and then to lend it to the government at 3 per cent. That is not good banking, if they are in the banking business.
I wish now to turn to the other side of this balance sheet. The land grant is dealt with there, but it is hard to understand and it is so uncertain that I do not propose to deal with it. But before I pass from the assets I wish to refer to that land grant, which is an enormous asset of that company. Its condition, Toughly speaking, is set out at page 17 of this report. The company has already received $79,000,000 out of its land grant, but it paid $36,000,000 in various kinds of costs, and the rest went4' into the equipment, but it has to-day a very large surplus in that land grant. The

total area of agricultural lands still owned by the company in connection with the original land grant is 74 million acres, but this is not included in the statement of the company's assets. It also owns 44 million acres from the British Columbia land grants. The statement does not set out how much of these lands are town sites. Probably the land grants, besides the $46,000,000 in the treasury and the money temporarily invested in government securities, would, together, be worth millions of dollars. So I would roughly say there are $85,000,000 to $100,000,000 of assets of the company to-day which could be realized if it disposed of its land grant. Here is this great company with all this accumulated cash on hand, and all this land grant that can be disposed of and enormous sums coming to it from those who bought lands but have not yet completed payment.
They have a treasury the like of which was never seen in any other country in the world. Never was so fat a treasury. The directors are lost when they try to do anything with it. And yet they fail to carry out their part of a solemn agreement to devote some part of that overflowing treasury to a reduction of the freight charges against which the people of Canada to-day complain. Any one who will examine carefully this statement of assets of the company will see that the company is enormously rich, and that it does not expose what its actual assets are. It never has done so yet, because it has never been asked to do so. If it is ordered by the Railway Commission to make such a statement, and such a statement is made, it will be found that that company has to-day anything from a quarter of a billion of dollars upward which it cannot use in the undertaking, which it has in some w'ay to switch away and give to its shareholders, but which is consecrated money. If ever there was money consecrated on the altar, the assets of that company are consecrated to a reduction of freight rates on the railway, and when the shareholders, those rich burghers of Holland, have their ten per cent, they ought to reduce their rates. They say:	We use it
for the building of other lines. They do not do that out of the treasury of the company. When they -want to build other lines, what do they do? When you look at their liabilities in that statement, let me tell you what they consist of:	Capital stock,
$150,000,000; mortgage bonds, $39,000,000; 4 per cent preference stock, $55,000,000 ; 4 per cent consolidated debentqre stock, $136,000,000. All these other millions are invested in the road besides the stock. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company has no difficulty in issuing debentures at 4 per cent to build any extensions they want. But they have an inclination to issue not only debenture stock, but common stock in

the shape of a melon to the shareholders, and now I want to come to that. This is what they have been doing. According to this last report they gave 7i per cent to the shareholders, making $10,500,000, and they gave a 1 per cent dividend on the land fund, making $1,500,000; or in all $12,000,000. That was at the rate of 8 per cent. By the report of last year, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company paid its shareholders 8 per cent and 8 per cent alone; and if called into court or into this House, they would say, that is all we gave. But I read in this House last session the statement of a shareholder in England, and it has never yet been denied, that for the last five years his return from his investment in the Canadian Pacific Railway Company amounted to 14 per cent per annum. Any one who wants that statement will find it in the Fin-eial ' News,' for the month of June, 1910. Now, what did the Canadian Pacific Railway give to its shareholders last year? It gave them the 8 per cent dividend, and as a melon it distributed amongst them pro rata 300,000 shares of stock at 125. It did propose to give it to them at par, and some months ago I started an agitation in this House against it. Whether that was efficacious or not, certainly when the stock came to be issued, it was issued at 125tand the consequence was that with the stock worth 175, or 50 points better than the rate of issue, $22,500,000, was distributed among the shareholders. That was exactly equal to 10 per cent, which, with the 8 per cent paid as dividend, made 18 per cent paid last year to the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific railway. I ask the people of the Canadian west, and the farmers of Canada generally, if they will say that that is what they expected the Canadian Pacific Railway shareholders to distribute among themselves last year. And in the evening papers of last night it is said that there is to be in a few days another issue of $20,000,000 of stock, so that if the shareholders get 10 per cent in that shape besides their dividends, another 18 per cent is in sight for the next year. No wonder the stock is going up; no wonder it is the finest stock in the world. But is the company discharging its obligations to the people of Canada as well as to its shareholders? Do the people of Canada intend that this game shall be continued forever? The dividend now is to be 10 per cent, according to Mr. Creelman; and for the last five years up to last year it was 4 per cent additional in the way of melons and bonuses of stock, and another melon of $20,000,000 of additional stock is to be issued in a few days. How long is this to be continued? Is this good policy? You can play this game too long. The stock issued now is $180,000,000, and that is to carry 10 per cent hereafter. It will soon be $200,000,000,
and if that is to pay 10 per cent, then every year out of the net earnings of the company $20,000,000 will have to be paid in dividends alone. The railway will not stand it; and yet they will go on and make other issues, until, if not interrupted, they will increase the stock to $300,000,000; and they build the extensions of the road out of shareholders' stock instead out of debenture stock. Eventually they will kill the goose that lays the golden egg, and they will get to a point beyond which they cannot go. All the financial crimes in connection with the railroads of the United States have their origin in the issue of new stock and the payment of bonuses to shareholders, so that to-day American railroad securities are without credit in the world. These things have not been done to any great extent in Canada as yet; but the great Canadian Pacific railway has started in to do them; they are paying bonuses and big dividends to their shareholders, while they are not discharging their duties to the Canadian public; and unless we take care to avoid it, our securities will be in the same position that American securities are in Wall street to-day. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company can get what money it wants for its undertakings by the issue of 4 per cent debenture stock, and its other earnings should be devoted to a reduction of the traffic charges paid by the people of this country.
Now what about the new company that was to be created for holding purposes? Perhaps one or two members of this House and one or two newspaper men headed it off. Perhaps it never was attempted, but every newspaper in this country said it was under way, in imitation of what had been done by certain notable financiers in connection with the Great Northern and other western roads in the United States. The scheme was to form a company-out of gift stock or paid up stock. I do not know-[DOT] of exactly the same shareholders as the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific railway and to switch all the lands a^y from the treasury of the Canadian Pacific railway and convert them into a great melon for those shareholders. Sir Thomas Shaug-nessy denied that in a way subsequently; but all the financial authorities in Wall street and London confidently expected that this new company was to be created out of the Canadian Pacific railway shareholders There was a similar temptation in this in stance to do what Jim Hill did in connection with the iron lands in Minnesota. If that had been done, all the land reserves and town sites, all the acreage now held by the Canadian Pacific Tailway would have been taken out of its treasury, and never -ould have been used as an argument for a reduction of rates. That, however, did not take place. Why, I do not know; but .

that it was contemplated I have every reason to believe. All this shows that while the Canadian Pacific railway have acted in a creditable way in some respects, it has not discharged the full obligation contained in that solemn undertaking in its original charter, under which the rates are always open to revision and ought to be revised when the treasury of the company can afford it.
This was a rather bold game to contemplate. It would have been a horrible example to set. The rate of interest is going up in this country and you have now to offer special inducements in order to sell securities. If you want to sell bonds in connection with certain propositions, you have to give a bonus of some kind, and things have reached such a pass that securities have not now the reputation they used to enjoy. The result will be to demoralize finance to the detriment of cheap money which is so essential to Canada. I may be told that the Canadian Pacific railway has set a splendid example. I say that it has set a bad example in attempting to switch away its lands from its treasury to another company and thus evading the law which enacts that the rates must be reduced when the treasury of the company can afford it.
That is pretty nearly my case. Then there is the question of regulating the capital of railway companies. That is to be my next proposition with which I propose to deal on a future motion to go into supply. I propose to argue that the capital of railways should be controlled by our railway commission just as it is controlled by the railway commission of New York state. That commission deals with municipal franchise in the State of New York. From 1907 to December last the total amounts of securities applied for in that state was $461,000,000 and the State commission approved of only $233,000,000, leaving $208,000,000 which they either disapproved or held in abeyance. In other words, wherever there is a commission regulating railway securities, the railway companies are not allowed to issue any securities, the proceeds of which are not devoted to the undertaking itself. There can be no issue in New York of securities the proceeds of which do not go into the treasury of the company. In that way the cutting of melons is prevented. It will be a crime of crimes if the Canadian Pacific railway should issue the remainder of its authorized increase of capital at less than market price. That $20,000,000 should be put on the market at the market price and the proceeds poured into the treasury and not have the profits go into the pockets of these lucky burgheTs of Holland, the descendants of the Van Tromps who swept the Zuyderzee with the broom at their mastheads. They like the game, it Mr. MACLEAN.
is fine for them and the other shareholders, but most expensive for the people of Canada, and one that will reflect no credit on this parliament if we allow it to continue, We cannot afford to have this kind of business continued in this country. We cannot afford to have the proceeds of any securities offered by any company swept into the pockets of the shareholdes instead of being used for 'the benefit of the undertaking; and if these proceeds, be used for the benefit of the undertaking, the result will be a reduction in railway rates.
I am now coming to another and a larger issue and one which has been raised before, and that in the enforcement of public rights under federal law. It was a federal law which created the Canadian Pacific railway. It was a federal law which created the Railway Commission, and it is the duty of this parliament to enforce its own laws and uphold the rights of the people as embodied in these laws. I have argued out this question with the present Attorney General, the right hon. the Prime Minister and others, and the result has not been satisfactory to me. I have been told that the principle which prevails here is different from that which holds in the United States-that the enforcement of federal laws, which devolves on the American government and Congress, devolves on the provinces in this country. Gradually, however, we have seen this happening in this House., We have seen the government of the right hon. gentleman compelled by public opinion to enforce the federal laws before the courts. My right hon. friend has instructed some one to go to the Privy Council with regard to an old clause in the organic act of the Canadian Pacific railway. We have had eminent counsel employed by him in vindicating public rights before the tribunals in connection with various organizations-such as the public rights with regards to telegraphs and telephones and express companies. But this, so far, has been done, as one of the German philosophers said of his theories, 'a3 the grasshopper jumps/ It has been a grasshopper policy, moving only as the grasshopper jumped.
Now, the day has come when the enforcement of public rights under a federal law becomes the first and greatest duty of the government. And I want to make this an issue between myself and any government of this country, between tne people and the government, and between the people and any political party opposed to the people's rights. The enforcement of public rights is a sacred duty devolving upon this parliament, and upon us as members of this parliament. In that view, I contend that it is the duty of this House to accept my motion, which is made in a non-partisan sense and without partiality. The effect of that motion is to declare that it is the

duty of parliament to take immediate steps to ascertain whether, in view of the enormous regular dividends-now 10 per cent, and this cutting of melons every few years which brings the returns of the shareholders up to 18 per cent-it is not the duty of this House to declare for immediate action to ascertain whether the people who pay these enormous dividends are not entitled to a reduction. As I have said, the Minister of Justice holds the view that our system is somewhat different from that of the United States. ' So much the worse for Canada,' is my comment on that. Let me read a few words that I have read before in this House from the Act. creating the Interstate Commerce Commission. That has proved to be the greatest public body in the world, almost. Our greatest public body, to my mind, is that commission in Ontario which is administering the Hydro-Electric power policy. We have followed the lead of the United States, and we have a good Railway Commission, and I give the government credit for appointing a good commission. But we want to widen their powers, as the farmers have said. What are the powers of the commission in the United States?
The commission is hereby authorized and required to execute and enforce the provisions of this Act

I am reading from the ' Interstate Commerce Law.'
-and, upon the request of the commission, it shall be the duty of any district attorney of the United States to whom the commission may apply to institute in the proper court and to prosecute, under the direction of the Attorney General of the United States all necessary proceedings for the enforcement of the provisions of this Act and for the punishment of all violations thereof; and the costs and expenses of such prosecution shall be paid out of the appropriation for the expenses of the courts of the United States.
Theirs is not so good an Act as. ours ; it is not so far-reaching ; but it is ten times better in that it provides for its due enforcement by the commission itself, through the employment of the deputies of the Attorney General and at the expense of the United States. Now, to show how great the reform feeling is in the United States, let me read a few words from a current review. That great republic has been on the verge of revolution, to my mind, because of high finance, in regard to railways largely, and because of disregard of public rights. But what I have here to read will show how rapidly they are changing things there. I read from the ' American Review of Reviews ' for this month. It will show what the great law officers there axe doing. And let it be remembered that we have here a Minister of Justice and an Attorney General, -and a 58
Solicitor General. The ' Review of Reviews ' says :
Not the least interesting of Mr. Taft's appointments last month was that of the Hon. Frederick W. Lehmann, of St. Louis, as Solicitor General of the United States. Mr. Lehmann is this year president of the American Bar Association, and his professional reputation is so high that if Mr. Taft had appointed him to the Supreme Bench there would have been general approval from the lawyers of the country. Mr. Taft was once Solicitor General himself, and he regards the office as of immense importance, especially at this time when great cases are to be argued before the Supreme Court. Mr. Bowers
That was his predecessor.
-had brought a great reputation from Chicago, and it wa.s supposed that Mr. Taft might sometime elevate him to the Supreme Bench. His death was a serious loss, and Mr. Taft fills the vacancy by the appointment of another lawyer of the Mississippi valley of equally high standing. Mr. Hoyt, who had been Solicitor General in the Roosevelt administration, was chosen by Secretary Knox as the counsellor of the State Department, and his death a few weeks ago marks another vacancy in the group of talented lawyers who have been giving the government their devoted service.
That is the great characteristic of the profession of law in the United States today-that the government has been able to command and the public life of the country has called forth, the services of the ablest lawyers for the defence of public right. That was not the case ten or fifteen years ago. Of all the changes, there is one so notable as to be almost a transfiguration, that of Elihu Root, once the counsel of all the raiding done in New York in connection with local transportation, counsel of the Whitneys, and of the Philadelphia exploiters of street railways, now a public servant and a defender of public rights. The government of the United States secures the services of these men, men of the highest training, to engage in the battle for public rights. I do not pass comment on our Canadian men in that respect further than to say that we have a good commission. In the United States men are training themselves to be public servants as a scientist trains himself for his business. And government to-day is a matter of science, a matter of efficiency, a matter calling for the best men for the public service. It is because they are securing such men for the bench, for public commissions, and as the heads of departments that these reforms in the United States are going on. And let me read you a paragraph about the Attorney General of the United States-the equivalent of our Minister of Justice.
It is a picture of great activity which is presented on behalf of the Judiciary Department. Never before in the history of the

country have the law officers been so busy in so many different directions. Mr. Wicker-sham's vigilance, with the aid of many trained assistants, has ranged from great prosecutions under the Inter-State Commerce and Sherman Anti-Trust Acts to the breaking up of ' bucket shops ' and the terrifying of the scoundrels who are using the mails to sell bogus stocks to small investors.
We had in this House the other day the question about the use of the mails to defraud the public, and it was shown to be the duty of the Attorney General to protect the public against the use of the mails to defraud the people. Well, in the United States they are doing all these things in the interest of the public. Look what the Attorney General of the United States did not long ago in compelling the Union Pacific, I think it was, to restore sixty million dollars to the treasury of the United States. Somebody said: Oh, that doesn't amount to anything, let whoever likes go after it, it is not the duty of the state to do so. Now, I raise that point here, and I especially appeal to the men of the west, whether it is not the first duty of this parliament to enforce the public rights that are existant under federal law, from this moment onward. If the Canadian Pacific railway to-day has this overflowing treasury, if it has, as a matter of fact, paid its shareholders eighteen per cent last year, and is preparing to make them another bonus of that kind, is it not the duty of all men who sit in this House to join together in passing this resolution of mine, which is absolutely non-partisan, insisting, as it does, on steps being taken at once to ascertain whether the people of Canada, in view of some facts that I have set out here to-day, are entitled to some reduction in the tariffs of these railways? They are excessive, the people have a grievance against them, a grievance that has been stated in various places. The government have investigated some of them, and the finding has been against the railways. Therefore, a further investigation must be sweeping, and must include all these charges, it must include telegraph charges. Now, the Canadian Pacific railway telegraph charges in the west are excessive-so I have been told, and so I have experienced. The express charges certainly are excessive, the sleeping car charges are excessive, and we are going to get a reduction in a few days, I am told. But we are going to get that reduction because of the activity of the Inter-State Commerce Commission of the United States. They have had the Pullman Car Company before them, and the Pullman Car Company have confessed that their charges are overcharges. The Inter-State Commerce Commission has compelled the Pullman people to come into court and confess that they are delinquent in this respect, and there is to be a reduction made Mr. MACLEAN.
some day this month in the sleeping car charges in the United States, and consequently in Canada, because the Pullman Company operates in Canada. If the Pullman Car Company is compelled to reduce their charges in Canada, then the Canadian Pacific railway will have to follow the example, and it will spread probably all over the country, and the action of the United States in procuring relief there will have its effect in this country. I wish some of the decisions of the United States would also be adopted on this side of the line; perhaps the International Railway Commission will help to bring that about.
Now, it does strike me that I have made out a strong case here to-day in behalf of the people of Canada. The time has come for some active intervention in forcing a reduction of tolls on the Canadian Pacific railway. I am not attacking that company in any respect whatever; I am simply asking for the fulfilment of a contract they have made with this country, a contract that had two wings to it, one wing to protect the shareholder and the other wing to protect the public. The shareholder has reaped his reward, he is getting his eighteen per cent to-day, but the citizen of Canada has not yet come into his own in that agreement. It is in his behalf that I make this motion, and that I now submit to the House. I will go further, and say that if anybody can suggest a modification of my motion that will assist in bringing about the object I have in view, I will be glad to accept it. In the meantime, I apologize to the House for taking up so much time, although I believe the importance of the subject fully warrants it.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext:
I will not be so modest on behalf of my hon. friend as he was on his own behalf. I would have read all that article ill the newspaper, and what he has failed to read I will supplement. I am more than Teady to compliment him on the energy, the industry and the force with which he has applied himself to all these questions that he has discussed in this House, not only to-day, but previously. I do not agree with a good many of his ideas, but his ideas may be right, nevertheless. This much I think we must admit, that the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) has accomplished something in this country in his agitation along the various lines that he thought to be in the public interest. It must be remembered that in comparing Canada with the United States we are a good deal younger than the United States. Our railways aTe scattered over as large a territory, with about one-twelfth of the population, and some of the conditions that prevail in the United States do not prevail in Canada, and remedies that might apply

in that country would possibly not be applicable in Canada. They might do good, or they might do harm.
I agree with him thoroughly that as Canadians we are all proud of the great transportation institution that bears the name of this country, the Canadian Pacific railway. That company, with all its ramifications the world over, is the greatest transportation company in the woTld. Its origin was not so roseate; in its early days it did not have such an easy task before it. But the ability exhibited by the men then in control of the affairs of that company, and the tenacity with which they adhered to the task they had undertaken, have made this transportation company very profitable to themselves, and a credit to the Dominion of Canada the world over. When the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was asking for its charter originally there was a divergence of view as to the bargain made with that company. Some people thought the terms given them were too liberal; but the country, through the then majority in parliament made that contract with this company. That they have grown immensely wealthy under that contract, I am not sorry, I am glad of it, as a Canadian, because the more successful these great undertakings are in this coun-ti'y the higher will stand the name of Canada throughout the world. The hardest blow that this country could get, and among the nardest blows it has received in the world, will be found to be the failure of the projects that have a public or semi-public name, or appearance. I take it for granted that every Canadian is proud, wherever he goes, to find the Canadian Pacific railway looked upon as one of the best managed, one of the sanest conducted, and one of the most successful transportation companies in the world.
I am proud of that. Still, the company having all this success must keep its obfi-gations with the people. There was nothing sure at all when the Canadian Pacific railway was launched, even in the minds of the most sanguine, that it would be a reasonable success and no person ever dreamt that it would be the magnificent success that it has been. It must be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that the development of this great country of which we are all proud to belong is due in not a small measure to the energy, the zeal, the courage and foresight of the men who had charge of the Canadian Pacific railway.
Now, with these things in mind, not as a condemnation of the company because they have prospered, but rather as something highly commendable, because Canada has been big enough and they have been sufficiently qualified to make this company a success, let us look at it for a few moments. The conditions when this 58i
contract was let were not the conditions of to-day. If the House will pardon me I want now just to recall what my hon. friend dealt with a moment ago to explain what I mean. Previous to 1881 the Railway Act of 1879 was passed and that Act contained a provision as follows-I will read it so that there will be no misunderstanding: section 17, subsection H:
The parliament of Canada may from time to time reduce the tolls upon the railway, hut not without consent of the company, or so as to produce less than fifteen per cent per annum profit on the capital actually expended in its construction, nor unless on an examination made by the Minister of Public Works of the amount received and expended by the company the net income from all sources for the year then last passed is found to have exceeded fifteen per cent upon the capital so actually expended.
We will take subsection 10 of the same Act.
Every by-law fixing and regulating tolls shall be subject to revision by the Governor in Council from time to time after approval thereof, and after an order in council, reducing the tolls fixed and regulated by any by-law, has been twice published in the 'Canada Gazette/ the tolls mentioned in such order in council shall be substituted for those mentioned in the by-law so long as the order in council remains unrevoked.
The contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in 1881 substituted the words ' ten per cent ' for ' fifteen per cent ' in that new Act. That is, it made the conditions five per cent more onerous on the Canadian Pacific Railway Company than they would have been under the general Railway Act.
More than five per cent.
Yes, it would be a third practically, or 33 per cent.
Thirty-three and a third per cent.

Yes, 33i per cent more onerous. That change became law at that time, and it must be remembered that there was no forum to regulate rates except the Governor in Council. The Governor in Council was the forum which regulated rates, and the then parliament, very wisely left the settlement of this question to the Governor in Council under the statute which formed the contract.
Now, going on a little farther, I find that provision was made in another contract made with the Canadian Pacific railway looking to the formation of the Board of Railway Commissioners. In the year 1897 an arrangement was made with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for taking over what is known as the Crowsnest Pass railway. It will be found in that contract,

or in the arrangement which forms part of the statute of 1896-7 that there was an agreement made by the company providing for a considerable reduction in freight rates which not only was to apply to the Crows-nest Pass, but generally to the Canadian Pacific railway in that territory. I will read subsection (d) section 1, chapter 5, of that Act:
That a reduction shall be made in the general rates and tolls of the company as now-charged, or as contained in its present freight tariff, wherever rates are now the lowest, for carloads or otherwise upon the classes of merchandise hereinafter mentioned, westbound, from and including Fort William and all points 6ast of Fort William on the company's railway to all points west of Fort William on the company's main line, or on any line of railway throughout Canada owned or leased by or operated on account of the company, whether the shipment is -by all rail lines or by lake and rail, such reduction to be to the extent of the following percentages, respectively, namely:-
It goes on to give a list of the reductions which were then made, of which I will give a few:
Upon all green and fresh fruits, 33J p.c.; coal oil, 20 p.c.; cordage and binder twine, 10 p.c.; agricultural implements of all kinds, set up or in parts, 10 p.c.; iron, including bar, band, can plates, galvanized, sheet, pipe, pipe fittings, nails, spikes and horseshoes, 10 p.c.; all kinds of wire, 10 p.c.; paper for building and roofing purposes, 10 p.c.; roofing felt, box and packing, 10 p.c.
It gives quite a long list.
Now, Sir, I am calling attention to this to show that the Canadian Pacific railway have had their rates reduced through government or parliamentary action before there was a Board of Railway Commissioners. In that same Act it is pointed out that there will probably be a Board of Railway Commissioners and to show that I will read subsection (c) of section 1, chapter 5:
That so soon as the said railway is opened for traffio to Kootenay Lake the local rates and tolls on the railway and on any other railway used in connection therewith and now or hereafter owned or leased by or operated on account of the company south of the company's main line in British Columbia, as well as the rates and tolls between any point on any such line or lines or railway and any point on the main line of the company throughout Canada, or any other railway owned or leased by or operated on account of the company, including its lines of steamers in British Columbia, shall be first approved by the Governor in Council or by a railway commission, if and when such commission is established by law, and shall at all times thereafter and from time to time be subject to revision and control in the manner aforesaid.
Perhaps I may read it wrongly, but it strikes me that that Act would bring Mr. GRAHAM.
the Canadian Pacific railway main line under the Board of Railway Commissioners when it was established.
It might.

At least that would be my contention. Perhaps it is not legally right, but it seems to me that it is fair proof that the very passage of this Act, and the acceptance of its conditions by the Canadian Pacific railway brought all their main lines and the Kootenay route under the Board of Railway Commissioners. It seems to have been the idea of parliament all the way through and it seems to be embodied in this statute that by the contract which was made with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company the Canadian Pacific railway would be brought under the Board of Railway Commissioners.

Was there any agreement executed by the company at the time of the passing of the Act such as that which the minister has just referred to?
' Mr. GRAHAM. I have not seen any such agreement.
It should be a schedule to the Act.

There must be some agreement in existence as they complied with all these rates as set out in this statute. It was a part of the contract, as I understand it, for the aiding of this line and_ the taking of it over by the Canadian Pacific railway that this statute should be passed and there must have been an agreement entered into although I have not seen it.
A little later, in 1903, the Board of Railway Commissioners was established. The Canadian Pacific railway at once raised the point that on account of their original contract with the government, made in 1881, they did not come under the Board of Railway Commissioners. I am not sure that that ground was well taken in view of the statute to which they became a party a little later. I think, perhaps, it was not well taken. I am inclined to think that the Act passed in 1879 brings them under the Board of Railway Commissioners. However that may be, the Canadian Pacific railway have contended that they weTe not under the Board of Railway Commissioners, under section' 10 of the original Act. In 1904, shortly after the establishment of the Board of Railway Commissioners, as I understand it, the Canadian Pacific railway contended that they were not compelled to come under that board. An order in council was passed to have the question settled by the Supreme Court as to the actual cost of construction of the Canadian Pacific railway. It must be borne in mind that although it is arguable that the rates should

be based on the dividend paid on the stock that that forms no part of the contract. The contract related to 10 per cent on the actual cost of construction of the ljne and it says so. If by their various steamship lines, and I submit, also, if by their sales of lands, if by the profits from the various ramifications of this great company the world over, they paid 15 per cent in profits, and they were not enabled by their profits from the railway itself to pay 10 per cent on the cost of construction, they would not be held liable under the contract if it was closely adhered to. But I do not wish to argue closely; we want to get the best rates we can for the people of Canada and this company is undoubtedly very wealthy. This case was going before the Supreme Court. It took some time, as the Minister of Justice pointed out I think a year ago in this House, it was quite an intricate case to settle on for reference to the court. Here was a road constructed 20 years ago, some of it before that, with all the various costs in connection with the construction with the rebuilding, with the rearrangement, with the change from wooden structures to steel and concrete, &c. Any person will agree with me that to go into the details of finding out the actual cost of that road would be a very long and tedious operation. When the case had been arranged for reference to the Supreme Court, Mr. Creel-man and the late Mr. Christopher Robinson, if I remember rightly, acting for the company, and Mr. Aylesworth, the present Minister of Justice, acting for the Crown, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick being Minister of Justice, an arrangement was arrived at by the then Minister of Justice and the solicitors of the company, that without any prejudice to the claim of the Canadian Pacific railway, they would raise no objection to the submission of their rates to the Board of Railway Commissioners, as was done by every other railway. In that connection Mr. Creelman wrote a letter in February, 1909, to the Minister of Justice as follows:-

Sir,-Referring to what has been said in the House of Commons on this subject and to your conversation with me on Friday afternoon of last week, I beg now to confirm what I then stated with reference to the position of the question referred to the court in connection with the 10 per cent toll clause arising out of section 20 of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's charter.
Pursuant to the agreement on the part of the company at the time the order in council was made in 1902 a case was settled and has been filed in the Supreme Court.
You will remember that owing to the many difficult points which arose a very considerable time was taken in settling this case.
About the time that it could be set down
for argument a number of rate questions were pending before the Railway Commissioners, which questions involved a reduction of rates upon the company's lines affected by the section above referred to.
Our company after consideration, although not waiving the benefit of the section, decided that no question would be raised under it in connection with the application then pending.
I conveyed an intimation to this effect to the then Minister of Justice and he expressed the opinion that so long as the company did not take advantage of the section there was not much object in proceeding with the case as the argument would be a very tedious and expensive one, and the taking of the accounts after the statute had been construed would involve enormous expense and continuous work for several years.
The position then taken by our company in this respect has been continued up to the present time.
With the exception of one case where the section was pleaded several years ago, and afterwards abandoned, the company has never in any rate application to the Railway Commissioners, sought the benefit of this section, but in every instance the commissioners have dealt with the applications on their merits and have treated our company, in this respect, in precisely the same way as and on the same footing with the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Northern and other Canadian railway companies.
Although our company is quite willing to proceed with the case, yet I am unable to see what good object will be served by doing so when the country is at present practically in the same position with regard to our rates as if the case had been disposed of by the court and every point determined against the company.
I might refer my hon. friend to just one other point to show that so far as the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners is concerned, he treats the Canadian Pacific railway just as if they were another railway without any rights that they may or may not have under the contract of 1881. A question was raised in a case of the Attorney General of British Columbia against the Canadian Pacific railway and the chairman of the commission used these words:-
Request was made that the board should cause an inquiry and have an account taken to ascertain if the earnings of the railway were such that the board could reduce the rates in view of section 20 above mentioned. This inquiry is not necessary as the company admits that its rates are subject to reduction or adjustment by the board if a proper ease-is made out.
