It would seem, notwithstanding all that has been said, that the company has, without prejudice, as Mr. Creelman points out_ to any rights they may have, acquiesced in the board having complete jurisdiction over their rates.

If I understood the minister, the company agreed that as regards

the matters that were then pending before the Railway Board they would admit the jurisdiction of the board. Then, in the matter just referred to, they again submitted to the jurisdiction of the board and the minister will recollect that the letter also says that in the agreement that was made in 1892 the company reserved their rights under section 10 of the original Act. Does the minister understand that the company had absolutely waived and abandoned all their rights under the contract and submitted themselves unreservedly in all matters to the board, or only that in certain cases they have submitted themselves to the board, reserving the right to take any position they might see fit at a subsequent date?

As I understand it, the attitude of the company is that they are submitting to the jurisdiction of the board, but maintaining their right under section 10, if they want to act upon it again in the future.

The minister referred to the fact that, by reason of the lapse of a very long time, it was a verv difficult matter to investigate and ascertain what was the actual cost of construction of this road. Does it not appear to him that if the company merely submitted itself from time to time and maintained the right at any time to invoke the original contract, the matter would become more and more difficult with the lapse of time, so that it would be much more difficult ten or fifteen years hence to have the position defined than it is now or than it was in 1902?

There is no doubt a great deal in what my hon. friend says. The situation would be cleared up entirely if the company said, we abandon our rights under that section if we have any. But if it came to a trial of the question whether the company had any rights under that Act, to my mind they would have a weak case. At the present moment they are raising no objection to the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. This contract was made at a time when we had not that forum for the settlement of these rate questions, though the creation of a commission was foreshadowed, and to my mind the Canadian Pacific Railway Company are stopped in that statute from claiming to be outside the jurisdiction of the Commission.
But they say they do not fear, but are ready to go on with the trial now. They say that in one of those letters.
I am not sure that they are so ready as that. However, the Railway Commission has complete control of rates in Canada. I agree with my hon. friend from South York, and I disagree with him.

I believe the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada is the best body, with the widest jurisdiction, of all such bodies in the world. I have had reason lately to make some investigation of this matter. In Germany, though the railroads are government roads, the freight rates there do not compare for one moment with the rates in Canada. They are three times as high as our rates. Their hauls are short, it is true, but their rates should be low, because their cars are all loaded. France has not approached the control of rates as we have. England has a board, but in the control of freight rates it does not compare with the Interstate Commerce Commission or with ours, and the control exercised by the Interstate Commerce Commission does not for a moment equal with the control exercised by the Canadian Commission. Our commission can take anything they like as a basis for fixing the rates of the Canadian Pacific railway; they can take the dividend paid on the stock or the actual cost of the road, or they can have the company file a tariff, which will be as they see it a fair tariff for the transportation of freight and passengers. Let me call my hon. friend's attention to another point. I am not defending the Canadian Pacific railway. But if you take the rates in the United States from the west to Duluth, and take the rates for a corresponding distance in Canada, you will find that our rates are lower in every instance. A statement which I had compiled last summer showed that the people in the United States were paying higher freight rates for the same distances than the people on our side. I have no hesitation in saying that, with all the power of the Interstate Commerce Commission, and with the great population in the United States and the great strength of their western railways, the rates to and from the west are higher than those in this country for the same distances. Being very much interested in this matter, it strikes me that whatever we are to do in this House, we ought to keep clearly in mind this fact, that we have established a board composed of able men. No part of the government of Canada does it more credit than the Board of Railway Commissioners. Their judgments are quoted as my hon. friend quoted them in the case of the express companies, and they have done a great deal of good; and I would not like to see anything done that would have a tendency to take out of their hands the complete jurisdiction we have given them, because they can exercise it better than we could and with more beneficial results to the people.

A very few words on the very interesting subject at present before the House. Un-

der the old Railway Act, notice was given to every railway company in the country that had received a subsidy from parliament that they would not be interfered with until their earning power was suffi-cent to pay 15 per cent upon their investment. In the arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company the Tate was reduced to 10 per cent, on account of the money and land subsidies and other privileges given to the company.
However, that has been altered and what is our position at present ? That position has been pretty fairly stated by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) . By the Act of 1897 and the agreement with the Canadian Pacific railway, we entered into a totally new arrangement. One of the 'Conditions was that we would have the power of appointing a railway commission for the purpose of fixing and regulating rates. Did that Act give this government absolutely the power to deal with the question ? I think it did. I think that the powers in the matter of rates were vested in the Dominion government independent of any agreement with the Canadian Pacific railway. I have my doubts as to what extent that would apply to the other railways of the country as we have had no legislation in that direction concerning them. The question is whether the Act establishing the railway commission supersedes the statutory offers or promises made to different railways in the country. As to our power, I have not the slightest doubt. No matter how solemn an agreement we may have entered into with any railway company, the power is vested in the Dominion parliament to abrogate that agreement at any time. It would be a bad policy and a bad precedent to do so, and no government will ever do it, if it can possibly come to an arrangement with the parties. But there is power in the Dominion parliament to do it if it likes. This parliament has the power to do wrong if it likes in that matter, but it will not do wrong wittingly. It may be the interest of the country, that the government should get. out of an agreement made with a railway company, but that is a matter of negotiation. Have they got out of the agreement made with the Canadian Pacific railway. I believe they have. I have not the slightest doubt that under the Act of 1897, and our subsequent legislation, the power is vested in the Dominion parliament of dealing with rates, but we divested ourselves of that power for our own convenience and vested it ,in the railway commission. Should we interfere with that P We should not, unless there he some real solid grievance to complain of. We have divested ourselves of the power and left it to that railway commission. Let the railway commission deal with it. The government have power over the railway commission as well as over
judges. The supreme power in this country is this parliament. Is it advisable that we should exercise it in this instance ? What reason is given for asking us to interfere ? We are given talks from the newspapers, expressions of opinion by delegations of farmers here and there, talks of certain manufacturing industries who complain of not being fairly treated. Is _ this the tribunal to .deal with such a question ? Have we not properly delegated the power of dealing with it to a commission; and if the commission should do wrong,_ this parliament has the power to supervise it. To my mind the commission has done right. The hon. gentleman says:	Lower the
rates. But a railway cannot lower its rates without the consent of the commission. When the commission was appointed, that was one of the points I put to the Minister of Railways, who introduced the Bill. Fix a maximum rate, I said, and let the railways do anything they like under that. Oh, no, he said, there would be then no use for a commission, there would then be an end to the matter and to a certain extent, he was right. If a railway had that right to make lower rates than other railways, would it not do it ? Give the Canadian Pacific railway power to lower the .rates and it will lower them to-morrow 5 per cent or 10 per cent. There will then be a nice fight on with ithe different railways and the result would be that the Canadian Pacific railway would be victorious in the end. We have guarded against that in the appointment of the railway commission by enacting that they .shall see that a fair rate is charged. Any one can go before that commission and say the rate is not a fair one and argue his case; and from the decision of the commission there is an appeal to this House. This House has the right and the power to supervise that commission. But we have the statement made that the rates are .too high, and it is made without any evidence, on nothing but hearsay. On this we are asked to pass this resolution. I think that possibly the hon.- gentleman is not serious, and that his intention simply is, to draw' the attention of the country to the matter.	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.
Until we have stranger reasons to .show that the commission have not acted in the interests of the country, the best thing we can do is to leave this matter alone.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I do not wish to delay the House, but this question is one which is attracting considerable public attention. My hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean), represents a certain phase of public opinion and his remarks

have considerable weight throughout the country. There can be no question that on every occasion he has been a fearless advocate of public rights as opposed to the rights of the various corporations which have encroached on the rights of the public. His work in that connection is well known in Ontario. His advocacy of the Hydro-Electric Commission, his strong advocacy of the doctrine of public ownership of public utilities and the public operation of those utilities, are well known, so that whatever he says, either in this House or in the journal he controls, has considerable influence on the people, especially in the province of Ontario, and no doubt on a large number of people elsewhere.
Knowing that in many cases he has fought as the champion of public rights in this respect, I have always given a great deal of deference to his opinions on any subject he brings before the House, because I feel that it is generally something new, and that in the end something effective will be accomplished. Sometimes perhaps it is brought forward with a view to obtaining a certain amount of publicity, again sometimes for the purpose of adjusting some matters which are burdensome to the people as a whole. Now, realizing that the member fpr York is to a large extent a champion of public rights, I have taken occasion to give some study to this question of the ten per cent clause in the Canadian Pacific railway contract. We all know, Mr. Speaker, those of us who read the public press, especially the American press, and more especially the American magazines, that for several years there has been a very fierce campaign carried on by those papers against what are called the corporations of the United States. Modern social development has resulted in the growth of great corporations owning vast assets, controlling vast sums of money, and on some occasions those corporations in the United States have been shown not to conduct their business with a view of benefiting the public. The result of this campaign has been that a number of those corporations have been brought to justice. In the case of the sugar corporation, I understand, a large fine has been imposed upon them, they have been found guilty of defrauding the government. The sugar trust, the tobacco trust, the Standard Oil Company, every one of these industrial corporations from the insurance companies down, have been attacked, and recently an attack has been made upon the American railways. Now, everybody knows, who knows anything about railroads and railroad companies, that for the past eight or ten years a great change has been taking place in the physical conditions of those railroads. The roads of the United States have been virtually rebuilt, and now in this country almost every road of any con-Mr. CURRIE (Simcoej.
sequence has been rebuilt. In order to rebuild those roads in the United States vast sums of money were necessarily expended for improvements. To meet these expenditures large issues of securities chiefly bonds were sold. It is claimed, perhaps justly, that some of the securities were issued without any reason, or that there were no tangible assets behind them. However, we find this condition existing at the present time, that the government of the United States has undertaken a prosecution, on a large scale of almost every large railway in the United States. Indictments have been drawn up against them, and what is the result? The result of all this agitation, the result of- these indictments, is that the credit of these railways has been shaken, in fact the credit of these companies, their power to obtain fresh supplies of money for improvements has been destroyed, public credit and confidences generally have been shaken, and business in the United States during the past year has been virtually at a standstill. In fact, they have hard times in the United States, in the midst of plenty, and a great many large industries, especially those that were dependent on the railways for their support, are virtually dormant, and a great number of workmen are idle. Now, it seems to me that possibly this agitation in our own country against our railroads is to some extent a reflex of the agitation of a similar character in the United States. In view of the critical condition of financial affairs throughout the world, compared with the happy condition we are in at the present moment in Canada, I consider that it is a very inopportune time for us to commence rocking the boat so far as our great corporations are concerned. That is my view of this question, it is only the view of an individual. But it would seem to me that if this House made any attack upon any of the larger corporations which are to some extent joined to the credit of this country, it would not only destroy the credit of those corporations, but it might bring hardship upon the country, and possibly a certain degree of hard times.
Now the Minister of Railways has discussed the ten cent clause. We all know, who have given any attention to this matter, that the Canadian Pacific railway was chartered by the Canadian parliament in 1881. This charter contained a clause, known as clause No. 20, which has been read by the Minister of Railways, and his interpretation of that clause 20 is to my mind correct. The interpretation that has been given by him also to the clauses of Consolidated Railway Act of 1879 is correct. It has also been shown in this House that at that time we had no Railway Commission ; it has also been shown that this question has been brought to the

attention of this House, and that the hon. gentleman who is now Minister of Justice brought an action before the Supreme Court to settle this matter of the ten per cent clause, and that action was suspended in the courts because the Canadian Pacific railway had given up its rights under this clause and voluntarily surrendered its rate schedules to the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. Now, my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) would have action taken to settle this ten per cent clause again.
No, I propose nothing of the kind.
Well, I presume that some action is to be taken.

Before the Railway Commission. I propose that the House express the opinion that steps toe taken to ascertain, under the Railway Commission probably, whether the time has not come, in view of the earnings of the company, to grant a reduction of rates.

Now, let us follow that out. Supposing that we had taken some action in this House on this ten per cent clause, supposing we had carried on a suit, as had been decided. The Canadian Pacific railway would have fought us on that ten per cent clause, and the result would have been that it would have taken ten or fifteen years for the government of this country to bring about a decision in the matter. The questions have been referred to the Privy Council, point after point ; it would have been contested at every step by the company, and no one would have got any satisfaction out of it except the lawyers. Now, what would have occurred during all this period that this fight would have been going on? The Canadian Pacific railway would have been charging any rate they pleased, and the result would have been that, instead of having their rates, as they are now, subject to the Railway Commission, they would have been arbitrarily fixed by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company themselves. My hon. friend from South York apparently, when he brought his motion before the House, did not know that the rates of the Canadian Pacific railway over the whole system were now under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission.
Mr. Speaker, I knew that absolutely, and I said so in the House to-day.
Then what does the hon. gentleman want by his motion?
Let the hon. gentleman read the motion, let him pay attention to what I said.
The motion says that some action must be taken. Is not that so?

I will read the motion.
That before the said motion be passed this House hereby declares that steps be at once taken to ascertain the rights of the public using the Canadian Pacific railway to a reduced tariff because of the provisions in that regard contained in the Act of parliament ratifying the agreement with that company, or any other Act.

Now, the hon. gentleman says that steps must be taken, he says they must be taken under the original Act. Now, under the original Act the steps must be taken toy whom? By the Minister of Public Works? I have got the statute here, the Minister of Railways has read the clause to the House, and you will find that the statute distinctly says, in subsection 11 :
-nor unless an examination be made by the Minister of Public Works-
That is, of the books of the company.
-of the amount received and expended by the company, the net income from all sources, for the year then last passed, is found to have exceeded fifteen per cent upon the capital so actually expended.
That would have been the procedure under the original Act, quite a difference from having the Railway Commission act. And if the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) had stated, in his motion that, the Railway Commission should take action to consider whether it was not advisable that the rates of the Canadian Pacific railway should be lowered under this 10 per cent clause, we could have understood clearly what was intended. Let us see whether or not the railway has earned its 10 per cent. We know that the Canadian Pacific railway is not only a railway company, but also a hotel company, a lumber company, a mining company, a land company, a steamship company-that it carries on a great variety of industrial operations. The hon. member has shown that there is something like $36,000,000 to the credit of the land fund alone. Mr. Creelman in his statement says .that the distribution this year will include 7 per cent from the earnings of the railway company. He does not say whether that includes the earnings of branch lines or not, but I suppose that those earnings would be included. Yet clause 20 only applies to the main line, which is virtually the only line mentioned in the original charter. But, suppose that this 7 per cent were all earned by the main line, what does the other 3 per cent_ consist of? If the Canadian Pacific railway sells land, distributes some of the money

with its annual dividend, or if it cuts down timber, sells it and distributes some of that money, or if it takes coal out of the ground, sells it and distributes some of the money -should that be considered a dividend in the strict sense of the term? I do not think that any man who understands finance would consider it a dividend. To my mind it is a distribution of assets. They certainly cannot grow more coal; they cannot take back the land they have sold; they might grow a second crop of timber, but none of us who are here now would be in a position to discuss any question arising out of such dividend disbursement after it had disposed of this second crop. It is clear that, if the railway company makes a distribution of three per cent from auxiliaries, these auxiliary revenues are large from the assets. That is really a distribution of assets. It has been shown tliat the company has, very wisely, expended a large amount of money received from land sales in the extensions of its branch lines. It is unnecessary for me to point out that the Canadian Pacific Eailway Company is one of the greatest corporations in the world. If its affairs had not been carried on properly and honestly from the beginning, it could not have succeeded. Any one who has had dealings with the Canadian Pacific railway knows that the company is always ready to meet and adjust matters and to deal fairly and honourably with everybody, from its humblest employee to its highest official. And if any individual from Pile o' Bones has a complaint to make against the road as to its rates, he can go before the Railway Commission and have the matter fought out even without a lawyer to help him. And the railway company has submitted to that; they have given away their position so far as the 10 per cent is concerned, and we have had the benefit of that concession for years. That being so, is there any necessity for us to stir this matter up? Is not this an inopportune time to discuss it? This railway company is the greatest advertising agency that Canada ever had. It carries on a railway business from coast to coast, but it also carries on a steamship business on the seven seas, its house-flag is found in every important harbour, and its agents are in every important port in the world. As a manufacturer,
I have received letters from many parts of the world as a result of the operations of these commercial agents, asking if we could provide certain articles of Canadian manufacture. We have had letters from Manchuria, from Hong Kong, from Bombay, from New Zealand, from Australia, from South Africa, from Genoa, from Vienna, from Antwerp. This railway company has its diplomatic service, its commercial agents all over the world, all working for Canada. And, beyond question, if Canada is to be a Mr. CURRIE (Simcoe).
great nation, not only in growing wheat, but in respect of manufacturing-and we ought to be great in manufacturing for we have the raw materials to make the greatest manufacturing nation in the world, if we only look after and conserve them-this outside service of the Canadian Pacific railway offers us the greatest commercial organizations in the world for profitably carrying on a successful foreign trade. There is no corporation in the United States or in the -world that can give you a through bill of lading to the four quarters of the earth as the Canadian Pacific railway can. The humblest shipper on the Canadian Pacific railway can get a through bill of lading to any place in the world. The company's agents will look after that shipment, and collect payment for him. While I approve of the hon. member (Mr. Maclean, York) bringing in a practical resolution calling upon the Railway Commission to investigate the rates of this road in accordance with the 10 per cent provision of its charter, I do not think the resolution he has introduced is sufficiently clear to reasonably command my support. I do not think it wise for us to start investigating unnecessarily the large corporations of Canada just now. It would be a serious matter if we carried on a campaign at this moment against all the corporations that are successful and that we have established by public credit. We have some corporations that are not acting properly and that might need investigation. But, the Canadian Pacific railway is not in that category. Under present financial conditions, a general campaign of investigation is not advisable. It may not be well for us to rock the boat when the storm is on, as at present. If we rock the boat and the Canadian Pacific railway or other corporations are injured, what would happen to the rest of the country? The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) we know is a good business man. He has had tremendous struggles, and has always succeeded, but not greater struggles than those of the men who were at the head of the Canadian Pacific railway, in the beginning for they pledged everything they had in the world, present and future for the success of the road. There should be a fellow feeling for them on his part. And as prosperity has come to this great road, so prosperity has come to him also, and he should have a kindly fellow feeling and not try to stir up that most disagreeable feeling happily found only amongst a few small Canadians, the fear that somebody else is going to make a dollar. This parliament should avoid discussions of that kind-that is my honest and firm opinion. Now, if the country is thr at-ened with this attack on corporations and on our financial system, we know that it is because the Canadian Pacific railway

stock is selling at such a high price in the foreign market. But it is for that reason that the country is so prosperous and so many people are coming in. Looking over ' Hansard ' of the old days, I noticed the speech of the late -John Charlton who figured out that, judging by the growth of the United States, it would take thirty years for the west to have 550,000 people in it. The silver jubilee, twenty-five years, of that road is about here, and the great west has practically over a million people in it, showing the intense life energy and the rapid growth of this country.
Now, coming to the question of freight Tates, anybody who has had to do with rates knows that the freight rates of' the west, as the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) has told us, are a great deal less than those in the western states. It is very well for men to come here as members of deputations to the Prime Minister and make all kinds of charges, and assertions, but I challenge any member of this House, the member for South York (Mr. Maclean) included, to take the schedules of the western American roads, in comparison with the schedules of the roads in the Canadian west, and prove that our rates are unfair or higher. That comparison will show that the Canadian rates are from five to fifteen per cent lower than the rates for similar distances on the American roads. Then, why stir up discontent? We had the announcement made in the press that the gentleman at the head of the Railway Commission, ex-Judge Mabee has dashed wildly ofi to Washington and is going to have a treaty made right away for an international Railway Commission. Now, as a shipper, I look on that [DOT]with a great deal of distrust. As a practical man of affairs, a Canadian, I do not want an International Railway Commission, because, from experience, I know that when the foreign railways have approached our Railway Commission, they have approached them not to reduce rates but to compel the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian Northern railway to increase their Tates in the west.
Everybody knows that it is only a few years ago since a case of that kind occurred with regard to the hauling of coal from Fort William to Winnipeg, and if these American roads had had their way the people of the west ever since then would have been paying 25 or 50 cents a ton more for their coal. Another evidence that the Canadian Pacific railway and other Canadian roads have lower rates than the American roads is the fact that' nearly all the foreign business goes by way of Montreal. Why is business increasing via Canadian routes? Why is it that the Oriental business of the great American roads now passes through Vancouver and over Canadian lines? We are
all willing that it may continue to do so.
I wish this House to understand that it would be a most dangerous thing to establish an international tribunal with power to govern freight rates. Then the rates would be the same from the Canadian west to the seas which the Kansas farmers has to pay. The Canadian roads would not have the right to make any reduction in the rates and the people of the west whoj are now clamouring so loudly for reduced; rates would have to pay from 25 to 30 per cent increased tolls on their grain and! other produce shipped east, in order that our rates might compare with the American rates. Let that question sink deeply into the head and heart of every member of this House. The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) is a gentleman who' gives deep thought to subjects of this kind. If he wishes he can compare the schedules and he will find out that wher-i ever the Interstate Commerce Commission of the United States has control of the rates the rates are higher than they are on this side. One question arises about reaping machines. It is said that the freight rate in the United States is less than the rate in Canada. That is quite true. The haul from 'Chicago to Winnipeg is shorter than the haul from Torontq or the east to Winnipeg, but compare it on the ton mile basis and you will find that the Canadian haul is cheaper. Let) us be just and fair and let us be Cana-' dians. We are threatened with all kinds/ of agitations in the press of this country. The press has virtually brought about a crisis in our affairs by demanding a reei-l procity treaty. I do not say whether it is right or wrong, I do not discuss it at the present moment as it may be discussed here in a few days. All I say is, let us be very careful before we undertake to make any changes in those great organizations that have accomplished so much and which were brought into being largely by the foresight of those men who sat in this House before us. Let us be very careful how we act and what we do. Let every hon. member of this House also, bear in mind that J. Pierpont Morgan said hot long ago that the man who was a bear on the success of the United States was bound to be a failure. I say here' that the man who is a bear on the future of this country is going to be a failure. We have every evidence that this country is going to be a great nation. We have more than doubled in ponulation over the percentage or ratio of increase that wasl laid down by Abraham Lincoln with reference to the United States. He issued a memorandum in which he foretold what the population of the United States should be a hundred years from then. We have beaten that ratio 100 per cent. Let us be

glad at heart because we will have more population in fifty years from now than the United States had after a hundred years of growth and development. Let us be true to Canada. Let us be contented, and happy, let us deal fairly and justly with all our great corporations, especially with this great corporation that has a reputation for dealing fairly and justly with every man, that is managed by Canadians, whose success has brought $300,000,000 of foreign money into this country in the last year and a half, to be managed not by foreigners, but by Canadians. Let us act fairly towards this corporation, let us be just to ourselves, let us bear in mind that in so far as the Canadian Pacific railway is concerned the less we attack it, especially on that most tender point on which a corporation may be attacked, that is with reference to its stock, the better it is for this country.
Now, the hon. member spoke about the stock question and he said that this rail-, way should build its branch lines with debenture stock. Everybody knows that debenture stock is really another name for a second mortgage, and that if you put a first or a second mortgage on a piece of property you have thereby established a fixed charge which you must pay or go into liquidation. He considers it wrong that in a very few years this road might' be building its branch lines out of the sale of its common stock. I wish every mile of the Canadian Pacific railway were built out of its common stock. Then there would be no fixed charges on the Canadian Pacific railway; there would be no interest to pay the bondholders, no capital to pay back. This road, it must be remembered;, has a lower fixed charge than any railway in America. Would it not be much better for this road to increase its common stock and sell its common stock, which does not give any fixed charge, or put any obligation on its propertv for the building of these branch lines than to go on issuing bonds and piling up indebtedness that must some day in the future be paid by whom?-the shippers. Apparently the hon. member for South York does not know the difference between debenture stock1 and common stock.

The hon. gentleman will pardon me; I think I do know. When he says that I do not know', I think that if he would come to school to me for two or three minutes I w'ould takel a good deal of the nonsense out of his head.
The hon. gentleman knows very well that I have been at school at his knee when I was a young newspaper man.
I am sorry for my pupil.

But I never learned until to-day from him that it W'as better for a company to put a mortgage on its property to build additions than to sell common stock at double its par value in order to make necessary improvements. Let us be just and fair with this road, do not let this House become stampeded on questions of this kind and let us get down' to the common sense view of things. If it is necessary, in order to clear the atmosphere, pass a resolution abolishing the ten per cent clause and leave the rates of the Canadian Pacific railway to the Railway Commission. Is it not better for this House to leave these questions alone at the present time when the bankers in Wall street are gathering and sitting up every night v'ondering whether another bank is going to go to smash or the financial world is going to come to an end. We as Canadians would be better to leave this question alone than adopt a meaningless resolution of this kind.

Mr. Speaker, the provision of the Railway Act of 1879 to which allusion has been made, was one that had been in force for a considerable time, when the Railway Act was revised in that year. It has already been quoted, but I may quote one subsection of section 17, in order to give point to what I am about to say.
The parliament of Canada may, from time to time reduce the tolls upon the railway, but not without consent of the company, or so as to produce less than fifteen per cent per annum profit on the capital actually expended in its construction; nor unless, on an exam-

ination. made by the Minister of Public Works of the amount received and expended by the company, the net income from all sources, for the year then last passed, is found to have exceeded fifteen per cent upon the capital so actually expended.
When the Canadian Pacific railway was incorporated in 1881 a section was introduced into the Act, which I need not quote, as it has heen quoted by several hon. gentlemen. The net result of that legislation was to give the government of the country a greater control over the rates and tolls of the Canadian Pacific railway than over those of other railways in the country. That is to say, in respect of all railways incorporated up to that date the government had the power of regulating the tolls after 15 per cent had been earned upon the capital. In respect of the Canadian Pacific railway, the government under the charter, incorporating the Canadian Pacific, railway, had power to interfere and to regulate the tolls after the company should have earned 10 per cent upon the capital actually invested in the road. I am not using the exact terms of the statute, but I have fairly stated the effect of the legislation.
The Canadian Pacific railway was proceeded with, it was built under 'the charter to which I have alluded, and some time later, about 1902 I think it was, the government of the country came to the conclusion that conditions had arrived under which it would be possible for parliament, under the provisions of the charter of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to regulate the tolls to be received for passengers and freight by that company. A statement of the case was prepared by counsel acting for the government on the one hand, and for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company on the other hand. The case opened up questions of very great complexity. It opened up questions of fact which would require a very prolonged examination before officers of the Supreme Court, a very long examination of witnesses, books and accounts. The case also opened up very difficult questions of law as to the construction of that statute, as to how the word capital, was to be construed. The net result of it, as I understand from the statement of the Minister of Justice, made about two years ago, and the statement of the Minister of Railways and Canals to-day, was this: The government, on the one hand and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company on the other saw that 'that litigation would undoubtedly be very costly and very prolonged if it were to be proceeded with. The Canadian Pacific railway and the government agreed that the case should stand over in the Supreme Court of Canada without being further proceeded with at present and that in the meantime, the Canadian Pacific Railway
Company should submit itself to the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission of Canada, as thoroughly and effectively as if that ease had been proceeded with and judgment given in favour of the contention of the government and against the contention of the railway company. I think that is a fair statement of the case, as I gathered it from what was said by the Minister of Justice two years ago and from what was said by the Minister of Railways and Canals to-day.	.
The actual situation, then, for five or six years past has been this, that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has submitted itself to the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, and has been subject to its jurisdiction just as thoroughly and effectively as any other railway in Canada. I would like to say one or two words about the situation in that regard. It seems to me to amount to this, that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has practically, although not technically, consented to judgment against it upon the case submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada for its adjudication. This is thoroughly satisfactory as long as it lasts; but it is perfectly plain and clear to all of us that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, for some reason, and under the advice of its counsel or otherwise, has reserved to itself the right at some future date to have that case proceeded with if it should deem it to be in its interest that that course should be pursued. That is the only criticism one can make with regard to the situation as it is at present. Now, if I might venture a suggestion in that regard, it seems to me that it ought to be the policy of the government to ask the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to make that temporary arrangement absolutely permanent and definite; and, if I might venture a word to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, I would say that in my opinion that great corporation, upon which so many well deserved eulogiums have been passed this evening, would be well advised to assent to that request without any reservation whatever, so that the Company^ would be permanently and definitely subject in every respect to the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, just a3 every other railway corporation in this country is subject to that jurisdiction. It seems to me that the government might very well press that pretty strongly upon the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and I think it would be wise for that company, and in their interest, to pursue the course which I have ventured to suggest. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company still has a technical right to have that question fought out in the courts and determined. For my part, I do not believe that company has

185S
the Board of Railway Commissioners to proceed to thorough inquiry into these matters. And the Minister of Railways and Canals, haying regard to his duty, would be hound, it seems to me, under these condition.*, to give direction to the .board for that purpose. Does the resolution proposed by my hon, friend from South York have any such direct purpose or aim as that? It has not. It is couched in the vaguest and most indefinite language. And, the fault I have to find with it, in conclusion, is that if my hon. friend is convinced that there is any real grievance in respect of the rates charged by this great railway corporation, he has not effectively challenged that grievance, and has not taken the proper course to have it redressed.

If the House will pardon me for a moment, I desire opportunity for a word of explanation in view of what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has said. That hon. gentleman has asked me why I have formed the resolution as I have formed it, and also why I proceed specially against the Canadian Pacific railway. In the first place, in the original Act, there was a distinction made between the Canadian Pacific railway and other roads, and a different rule was applied to the Canadian Pacific railway from that applied to other roads. In the second place, judged by the original Act, profits were to govern the regulation of tariffs, and I think I proved this afternoon that the profits of this road were exorbitant. As to other grievances, I leave these to the western members. If they do not say there are grievances, we may assume that grievances do not exist, or it may be for me, on a future occasion, to deal with the matter ; but the opportunity is here, and these gentlemen can do what they like about it. I -agree with what the leader of the opposition said as to the enforcement of federal law. He said that I did not refer to it. That was the point of my remarks this afternoon-that federal law Should be enforced by federal authority. The hon. gentleman acknowledges that he believes this ; so, thank God,
I have made one convert in this House.

I am much obliged to my hon. friend for his compliment, but I think I have already expressed myself three or four times in this House in the same sense as I have done to-night. So far as he sought to make any distinction between this railway company and others in Canada, I do not appreciate that distinction. All these railways are subject to the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and it is idle to attack one unless that you show that that one is charging unjust rates or higher rates than the others. My hon. friend has not attempted to do that. Therefore, I said, that if this motion pro-Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
ceeded at all, it should proceed against every railway company in Canada, or, at all events, against the great railway systems, the Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern, because we have not been shown that any grievance exists in respect of the Canadian Pacific railway, which does not exist in respect of the other companies. All are equally subject to the jurisdiction of the same tribunal, and the proper course would be to ask the proper tribunal, constituted for that purpose, to deal with the rates under its wide and extensive powers. It is manifest to all of us, I think, that this parliament, or any committee of this parliament, could not make an effective examination into the rates of the great railway corporations. We have not the expert officers, we have not the technical assistance, we have not the machinery generally for making such an examination. But we* have constituted a tribunal that has all these aids, and which can make that examination effectively if its attention is directed to any grievance or series of grievances from which the public are alleged to be suffering.

I do not altogether agree with the reasoning of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) that the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) should not have moved his resolution asking for the rights of the public using the Canadian Pacific railway because it was directed against the Canadian Pacific railway only. Because, if there was a grievance to be investigated, or a condition of facts which warranted parliament making an inquiry, the fact that investigation was confined to one particular railway was no reason why it should not be entered upon.

My hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald, Pictou), is misquoting me. What I said was that unless you show some special grievance arising in respect of the Canadian Pacific railway, there is no mere reason for investigating that than any other railway company.

I thought I was making myself clear, that I do not agree with the reasoning of my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) in that regard. The hon. membex for South York submitted what he thought was a good reason under the Act confirming the agreement with the Canadian Pacific railway in the first instance, why parliament should move. I say that I thmk he had the right to move that resolution if he was prepared to make any ease, and 1 do not think it was any answer to him to say : you have only moved against the Canadian Pacific railway. For, if there is ground to move against the Canadian Pacific railway the fact that other companies may be in the same position is no

reason for inaction. The hon. member for South York is to be congratulated, in some sense, for having brought this resolution before the House. But, now that he has discovered from the argument and discussion before the House this afternoon, that there is really no occasion for the House to interfere he should withdraw his motion and follow the views expressed by the leader of the opposition. One of the usually accepted theories in this country has always been that when the Canadian Pacific railway reached the point that it declared a ten per cent dividend almost automatically there was to follow a reduction of rates. That is the view that has been entertained by many people in this country, and it would almost seem as if my hon. friend from South York also entertained that view. But when one studies the Acts and statutes passed by this parliament it becomes at once apparent that the amount of dividend which may be declared from time to time by the Canadian Pacific railway is not the testing question, and it is not by reason of the fact that any such dividends may be declared that the right to deal with the rates follows. There is a great difference between the declaration of a ten per cent dividend and the right of parliament to interfere in regard to the question of rates. What does occur is that parliament can interfere when ten per cent per annum profit on the capital actually expended in the construction of the railway is obtained, not when a ten per cent dividend is declared by the company. Now, what is meant by that ten per cent per annum on the profit of the capital actually expended on the construction of the railway? That Act was passed in 1881, chapter 1, of that year. Later on in the same year an Act was passed which defined the meaning of the word ' capital,' chapter 24 of that year. An Act to amend and consolidate the Railway Act. I do not think my hon. friend from South York this afternoon was able to give the House any reason, legal or logical, according to ordinary principles, which would lead us to suppose that,..interpreting that legislation and subsequent legislation dealing with this case, the right to interfere has as yet arisen, or that parliament had any legal right under the agreement with the Canadian Pacific railway to interfere.
Does the hon. gentleman admit that I had a right to bring it before this House under the original Act?

What I say is that my hon. friend furnished no argument, legal or otherwise, which would lead any one who followed his argument closely, as I did, to suppose that the time had arrived when the right to interfere had arisen under this Act.
Not even by exorbitant profits?

It is not a question of profits, it is a question of the legal construction of these Acts, and the interpretation of the various statutes bearing upon this matter. They are of the mpst involved character. My hon. friend did not deal with that question in such a way as to impress me, at least, with the idea that he had so mastered it as to justify him in calling upon parliament to interfere. But assuming that my hon. friend had made out a case of that kind, in what body would jurisdiction rest to deal with it ? He did not indicate that. I may be permitted to indicate a logical way. In the original Consolidated Railway Act of 1879, it . would appear that if the right to interfere had existed at any time, it would have to be exercised after a report of the Minister of Public Works, who had investigated the subject. I assume that at that time there was no Ministry of Railways in existence, although, I may be mistaken. But whatever rights existed under the Consolidated Railway Act as to an investigation into these questions of tariff and rates, by a Minister were swept away by the legislation of 1888, which provided for matters of that kind being dealt with by a committee of the Privy Council. Hon. gentlemen will recollect that during the years which followed from 1888 to 1903 numerous questions affecting the Canadian Pacific railway and all other railways were dealt with by that committee of the Privy Council. By section 306, chap. 29 of the Act of 1888, the Canadian Pacific railway was declared to be specially under the jurisdiction of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council in regard to the tariffs and all the numerous questions set out in detail in that statute. Then in 1903 unquestionably the right to deal with tariffs and with all matters of rates was committed to the Railway Commission, and has been exercised ever since by that body. And supplementing the statutes uipon the subject, we have the adhesion of the Canadian Pacific railway to the principle that the Railway 'Commission should deal with the questions of rates; and as pointed out by the leader of the opposition, that body can review the rates and deal with them in every respect. So there is a means at hand by which the end can be attained which the hon. member proposes to attain by this resolution. If my hon. friend wants relief in that respect for those who suffer from high rates, the Railway Commission is at hand, and the remedy is there. The grievances of which he complains can be remedied, and are being remedied, upon the application of anybody who is affected. I am sure that the House and the country have profited by this discussion, but I do not think



my hon. friend has shown that the right of this parliament to interfere depends upon the payment of a ten per cent dividend, but rather it depends upon an involved consideration as to what was a ten per cent profit upon the capital actually used in the construction of the work, and upon other considerations of that character. And now that the question of higher rates is being dealt with by a body appointed by this parliament, it seems to me that my hon. friend has no longer any reason to press his resolution, and that he ought to withdraw it.

I have no desire to enter into a discussion of all the questions that have been raised during the discussion of this amendment. If I understand the argument of my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean), correctly, it is a burden of taxation of which he complains, and he would seek relief for the people from that burden. One feature of his argument was that it was a great drain out of this country to the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific railway living abroad, and that there was no way of imposing upon them any taxation, or compelling them to make any rebate of the admittedly large dividends which they received. Now I always listen attentively to my hon. friend, and I admire his zeal. It seems to me that this is the time and this is the hour when we need in this country a David Lloyd-George, and I am sure my hon. friend from South York would fill the bill. The complaint, as I understand it, in Great Britain was that there was too much money lying unused, and upon which there was no burden of taxation imposed. My hon. friend's argument here this afternoon was that we have great railway magnates, those who hold large interests in railways, and that they are not making any return, either to the federal or the provincial treasuries.
The mover of this amendment should' have devised some scheme whereby the' government should be called- upon to impose upon these shareholders a burden of taxation which would make some recompense to the country for the great ad->
vantages that were accorded to the sharer holders of that company. After all, the main point in this discussion is perhaps that it is the survival not of the fittest but of the strongest and that if we were to attempt to do what my hon. friend, would propose to do, if we were to attempt by parliamentary enactment to have rigid and fixed rates, we would be doing perhaps a wrong to some corporations which could not bear the burden. The Canadian Pacific railway, by reason of the1 past, of which none would wish to complain, bv reason of the advantages and circumstances which existed a quarter of Mr. MACDONALD.
a century ago, received from the people of this country an immense franchise not at that moment contemplated to be of the value that it is found to be to-day. But it is of immense value to-day and we must deal with conditions. I am not taking issue on the question raised as to what parliament might or might not do, or as to what parliament should or should not do, but I think my hon. friend is creative enough, constructive enough, inventive enough, to devise a scheme and embody it in a resolution whereby the people of this country could receive some return for the immense advantages they were given at a time, properly, perhaps, when we had no adequate idea of the immense wealth we were conferring. It does seem to me that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) has made a very strong point in stating that there is no particular reason why we should select the Canadian Pacific railway corporation from among the many. If there are other corporations which have received or which are receiving advantages they should be made to pay for them, and I think that I would repeat my suggestion that we have a David Lloyd-George rise up in Canadai to remedy the conditions of which thoi hon. gentleman has so strongly, so eloJ quently and so forcibly complained this afternoon.
Amendment (Mr. Maclean, York) negatived, motion agreed to and House went into Committee of Supply.

speechtext: This, Mrr Chairman, is for the purpose of providing a public building in the town of Megantic. A site has been bought, situated on Maple street, 64 by 132 feet and the proposed building is required for post office purposes, &c.
What is the building to cost?
The total estimated cost is $29,116.87. That includes the contract, fittings, furniture, lock boxes, side-; walks, fencing, contingencies and superintendence. The building is under contract! now.

Mr.' PUGSLEY. The postal revenue of Megantic is $2,637.78, and of Agnes $443.60 in 1909. In Megantic there was an increase last year of about $100.

Montreal, eastern postal station, $20,000.,

^ Mr. PUGSLEY. At the corner of St. Catherine and Plessis streets.

From Mr. Napoleon Jeanett, for $33,000. The property consists of cadastral lots 353 and 354 with a frontage on St. Catherine street of 72 feet and on Plessis street of 96 feet with a depth of 81 feet on the east line. That would be an area of about 6,500 square feet.
About $6 a square foot. Has the money been paid and the transaction closed?

Yes.
- Mr. AMES. What steps were taken to ascertain whether the price was a proper valuation?
Our usual course is to send an expert from the department to value the property, and I am satisfied that was done in this case.
Who are the architects?
Mr. J. Perrault, of Montreal.
Was there any competition or anything of the kind?
No. One reason for his employment was that there is a great deal [DOT]of work in the department, and the staff has not been able to overtake the work.
On what terms is he employed, a commission basis?
I have not that information here.

I feel quite sure that they have. I saw some plans myself and I think there is no doubt they have been approved of by the department.

The instructions are that the estimated cost shall not exceed $70,000.
Is there any penalty on the architect if they come to double that amount?
No, that is a matter for the chief architect to satisfy himself upon .before letting the contract.
I understand it represents about $100,000 expended.

Yes, a little over $100,-
000.

When does the minister expect it to be ready for occupation?
Mr. ^PUGSLEY. The contract has not been let yet. We will have to advertise for tenders, and I would suppose it would take 18 months at least to complete the building.
Montreal general post office, enlargement, additions and alterations, including fittings, furniture, &c., and alterations to old building, $140,000.

This is to make provision for a renovation of the old portion of the Montreal post office. Members are aware that a new building has recently been completed to form part of the Montreal post office. That building extends through to Craig street crossing Fortification lane, and is connected with the old portion of the post office by closed galleries. Tt has been decided that the old building shall be renovated so as to make it as nearly fireproof as possible, and at the same time to give it an appearance in harmony with the new part.
The same style of architecture that prevails in the new building will be followed?
So far as it can be done.

The work is not under way yet. It will be done, I presume, by contract so far as work of that character can be done by contract.
Is there an architect?

No, these plans are being prepared by the department, and will have to be supervised by the department. Possibly a local architect will be appointed, but that has not been decided.

Yes, there were two tenders, this one at $4,600, and another, at about $6,200.
Montreal new barracks, $100,000.
This is to provide for the erection of a new barracks for a unit of the permanent corps in Montreal Military District No. 5, which has been requested by the Department of Militia.
Where is it proposed to build the new barracks?

At Longueuil. The sum of $200,000 was received from the city of Montreal for the sale of St. Helen's island, which was owned and controlled by the Militia Department, and this amount will be used for the purpose of erecting a new barraoks; but, of course, we nave to include that amount in an appropriation, although it has been received from the sale of another property.
Does that mean that the old buildings on St. Helen's island will be entirely removed?
I am not sure, but I presume so, because the island has been sold to the city of Montreal.

About three-fourths of the island was formerly a public park, and the northeast side was used for the old barracks, and I wanted to know whether the government, in relinquishing the island, expected that the old fortifications would be demolished so that the park might be enlarged.
I presume that will be the case, because the whole island has been transferred to the city of Montreal.
Has the land at Longueuil been purchased?
It has been owned by the government for a great many years.
How much land is available for the purposes of a park?
190 acres.
What troops are going to occupy these barracks?
It is to accommodate one unit of the permanent corps, consisting of 46 officers, 340 non-commissioned officers and men, and 114 horses.
Where has this unit of force heretofore been accommodated?
I am not able to tell my hon. friend. Would my hon. friend aliow me to get that information for him and furnish it to-morrow?

I think it is a great weakness that when the estimates are going through, though the minister in charge is able to give information in regard to his own department, yet when anything is asked about another department he is unable to give the information, and the minister of that department is not present. There are only two ministers here to-night. I am of opinion that the item should stand until the whole information can be given.
Ordinarily speaking, that may be correct, but upon my promise to give the information the hon. member for St. Anne seems to be satisfied.
If the hon. minister cannot give us the information on that item, he should let it stand until he can give it, and go on with some other item.
When the hon. member for St. Anne, who is interested in this matter, acquiesced in my suggestion, I think other hon. members might concur in it.

I do not think that is fair. Other hon. gentlemen may be interested in getting the information, and until we know what that information is we cannot judge whether the item is one that should go through or not. When the information comes down it may or may not require some criticism. The information might furnish the very best reason why the item should not carry. It might be such as to horrify even the minister himself and cause him to move to strike out the item. We want to be reasonable, but when information is asked foT I do not think the item should pass until the information is brought down.

I did not acquiesce in the item passing before the hon. minister gave us the information. I asked what forces were to occupy these barracks and where they were previously. We have had some hope that we might have a military school at some time in Montreal, and it might be a question whether the best site for it would be at Longueuil. I do not know what this building is to be occupied

for, and therefore am in no position to offer any judgment as to whether this is the test site. I think it would be only fair, before the item passes, that we should know the facts.

This is to accommodate a portion of the permanent force, one unit of the permanent corps in the Montreal military district. The accommodation to be provided is for 46 officers, 340 non-commissioned officers and men and 114 horses. As regards erecting these barracks, that is a matter of good faith with the city of Montreal, because when Montreal paid to the Militia Department $200,000 for St. Helen's island, where the present barracks are situated, it was part of the understanding that the money should be utilized for the erection of new barracks in Montreal or its very near vicinity.

The hon. minister of course understands that I am not objecting to any undertaking made with the city of Montreal being carried out, but to be told that these barracks are to be occupied by one unit of the regular force gives us very little information indeed, and puts us in no position to judge whether the erection of a barracks in Longueuil is the best way to carry out the undertaking that a barracks should be erected in Montreal. What are you going to do with that military force?

I have no objection at all to letting the item stand, and no doubt 1 shall be able to get further details from the Militia Department.
Item allowed to stand.
Napierville public building, $10,000.
This building is expected to cost in all not more than $15,000.
What is the population?
Nine years ago it was about 800.
What is the revenue from the post office?
What rental have you been paying?
$44 per annum.
Would it not be better to continue at that rental than invest $15,000.

The accommodation at present is inadequate. There is quite a business in money orders. Last year the money orders issued amounted to $18,776. Napierville, though not a large town, is a town where there is quite a little manufacturing industry, and it is rather a thriving place.	.	.
Does the minister not think that $15,000 is a liberal sum to give for a building in a town where the revenue is only $735?
We calculate that the site will cost about $2,000, leaving $13,000 for the erection of the building, including, heating, plumbing, lighting, fitting and everything.
What is the size of the lot?

The site is not yet purchased. We have been urged very strongly by the town of Napierville to erect this building. We have been urged by petitions sent in and transmitted to my department by the Post Office Department. The probable expenditure for the site will be $2,000 but we have not yet purchased it.
The hon. minister says that a petition was sent in. Does it influence his department to a very great extent?
So far as the facts stated are concerned, it does.
Will the hon. gentleman read the petition?
There seems to have been a vote of $5,000 last year and the minister says he has not bought the site yet. What has become of the $2,000?
It is expected that the site will be purchased before the close of the fiscal year. That will take $2,000, leaving $3,000 to revote. We still have the $2,000.
Where is the town of Napierville?
In Laprairie and Napierville.
Is it a shire town?
Yes.
Is it incorporated?
Yes, because it .has a mayor.
Is there to be a custom house there too?
No.
From whom was the petition?
From the mayor and other citizens of Napierville. It was sent my department by the Post Office Department as long ago as September 18, 1909.
Was there no request from the sitting member?
I have no memorandum of any but I know he urged it also.
Any letters or correspondence from him?
I have no memorandum of any?
Has the hon. minister a site in view?
The deputy minister says he cannot recall any reports on the site.
Is not $2,000 a most extraordinary sum for a site in a village of 700 people?

It depends a good deal on the location. The place had a population, in 1901, ten years ago, of about 800. It is probably now .a place of about 1,000 people. Get a site in the .business centre of a town of that population, and I am not prepared to say that $2,000 would be out of the way. What we do in most cases is to send an expert to examine the different sites available and compare them and test the prices with recent sales, and make his report.
Has that been done in this ease?
No.
How is the amount arrived at?
We assume that the site may cost $2,000, and we ask for a revote of $3,000. If we do not use it before the close of the year, the vote will lapse.
Will the expert be heralded when he goes to the town as the man representing the Public Works Department, who has come to buy a site for $2,000?
If my hon. friend has had any experience-

Yes, I have had some experience.
Mr. PUGSLEY-he knows that this gentleman moves cautiously, and is thoroughly reliable.

Every person knows that when the Department of Public Works, with millions behind it, sends an expert to purchase a site, it is charged about three prices. Instead of sending a representative in this way, if the minister would quietly ascertain what situation would be acceptable to thle people, and purchase in tlie ordinary way, he could get a site for one-third or one-quarter of what he now pays. In the town of Whitby they paid $5,000 for a site, and they could readily purchase a better site to-day for $2,000. But, in order to placate a political follower of the hon. gentleman in charge of the department, they paid this higher price. The history of the purchase of that site will come out, no doubt, when these affairs are investigated, but the facts are Mr. BLAIN.
simply these : The gentleman who was the owner or mortgagee of the site was offended on account of Mr. Leonard Burnett being set aside ' at the instance of ' the present member (Mr. Fowke) for the riding, and to placate him and retain his political friendship they gave him $5,000 for his property.
Does the hon. gentleman say the site was bought from Mr. Burnett?
No, from Lyman Barclay, who was the mortgagee or ostensible owner-at any rate, the man who got the proceeds.
That would make him more than the ostensible owner.
It may have been put through in the name of the Sons of Scotland, but Mr. Barclay got the proceeds.
If Mr. Barclay was the mortgagee, were the Sons of Scotland the owners of the equity of redemption.
It may be that the Sons of Scotland were the mortgagees, and this gentleman the owner of the equity of redemption.
Then he would be more than the ostensible owner.

At any rate, the minister paid him nearly three prices for the site in order to get him into line and support the present member for South Ontario. And that method of purchasing a site is being followed all over the country. Hon. gentlemen opposite are utilizing the public treasury to put money into the pockets of their political followers. A representative of the department comes to the town and holds himself out as the representative of the Public Works Department, and pays from four to seven times the value of the site in order to play into the hands of the minister's political supporters. The' minister should purchase sites for the public as he would purchase them for himself, or as a railway company would purchase them. Sending a secret agent or representative of the department, they could get options on sites at reasonable prices, the prices of the open market for these properties, and would save hundreds of thousands of dollars to the country.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sharpe, Ontario) comes from the wilds of North Ontario, and may well be excused if he knows nothing of the values on the front or in South Ontario. The statements he has just made are absolutely misleading and quite unreliable because untrue. The gentleman from whom the site was purchased, was not a disaffected Liberal. The
18G9

time has never been when Mr. Barclay was anything hut an enthusiastic member of the Liberal party. The purchase was not made from him to placate him because of ill-feeling entertained towards the present representative of the riding, or any other Liberal, so far as I know.
He was the owner of the property?

I do not know whether it was owned by him or by the Sons of Scotland, but he was interested in it. If the statement made by the hon. member for North Ontario is a fair sample of the statements hon. gentlemen opposite are making everywhere in relation to the purchase oi' sites for public buildings by this government, they are to be discounted wholly. The site was bought at a proper price. It is the most eligible site in Whitby, directly opposite the Dominion Bank, a property worth $20,000. Public bodies of the town of Whitby endorsed the purchase of the site at the price paid. I canvassed the Conservative business men of the town, as well as the Liberals, and, with one single exception, they all said that it was the only site suitable for a public building in the town and was cheap at the price. And some of them said that if they owned the lot they would not take twice the price paid for it by the government.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowke) speaks of my not knowing the value of sites in South Ontario, as 1 come from the ' wilds,' as he says, of the north end of the county. I may say that the values in the north part of the county exceed those in the south end. I am perfectly familiar with the values in the south end. As to the site that is under discussion, there was a frame building on it, and the government paid $5,000 for the land, allowing the owner to take away the building. On the opposite corner there is a site equally desirable with a solid-brick building, and the whole property can be purchased, I am told, for $2,000. That is what is told me by a reputable citizen of Whitby. The gentleman in Whitby from whom the purchase was made by the government stated publicly that he would not support the hon. member who now represents the riding. It was known all over the riding that, owing to the way the hon. gentleman made Mr. Leonard Burnett, the previous member of the rfding resign his position as nominee of the party, Mr. Barclay was disaffected, and would not support the present representative. It was up to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowke) to placate Mr. Barclay, and he went to the Public Works Department, and got that department to pay Mr. Barclay $5,000 for a property that was not worth $2,000. These are the facts.

It is too bad to have to follow such statements as the hon. gentleman has made. I wish to say with regard to the statement he has made concerning myself and Air. Leonard Burnett, that I had nothing whatever to do with Mr. Burnett's declining to be the candidate of the Liberal party in South Ontario.
You opposed him in the convention.

I did nothing of the sort,
I did not oppose him at the convention.
From whom did you get the nomination?
I got the nomination from the Liberal party.
Why did Mr. Burnett resign?

It was eight years ago that Mr. Burnett resigned. Air. Ross was here for four years; after that Mr. Christie was here for four years. The hon. gentleman does not know what he is talking about, and he is misrepresenting the circumstances entirely. What he says is an absolute untruth.
Some hon. AIEMBERS. Take it back.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of order is raised.
I submit to your ruling.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have not ruled yet. The use of the word ' untruth ' is undesirable in the House, but the word ' untruth ' is not necessarily out of order. It will depend upon the manner in which it is used, whether it conveys the idea of an intentional untruth, and it is only in that case I rule it to be out of order. [DOT]

What I intended to say was that the reflections which the hon. gentleman cast upon me were uncalled for, and that in no instance had 1 given the slightest occasion for the representations which he made regarding myself and Mr. Leonard Burnett. I wish to say moreover that I never had an ill word with Mr. Lyman Barclay in my life, that I never spoke to him in the Public Works Department in relation to the purchase of the site.
You are taking all the credit for it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish to point out that there is an increasing custom of addressing hon. members of this House in the second person. When an hon. member wishes to address another he must do so through the Chair. The use of the pronoun * you ' is not allowed.

Before the item passes I would like to ask whether it is the policy of the Public Works Department that, in towns of 800 population, they

are willing to erect post offices costing $15,000. If that is the policy, then there are many towns throughout the older provinces with 800 population that are likely to have post offices showered upon them costing $15,000. I would like to hand ii to the minister the names of a number o towns of 1,200 or 1,500 that are badly in need of post offices.
Mr. PUG8LEY. There is no policy such as the hon. member mentions, of showering public buildings throughout the country In fact, a great deal of my time is taken up in considering applications, and in sifting out those which seem to be most urgent from * a public standpoint, and either rejecting or postponing other applications.
were grant all the applications which are placed before us, it would taki a great deal more money than the Minister of Finance places at the disposal of my dte-partm-ent. In the present case, Napier-ville is the shire town of the county, and is in addition a thriving place. We do feel that some distinction ought to be made in the case of a shire town, and where there is already no public building m the county. If the people of a town come to me and represent that there is no public building in the town, that it is the shire, town of the county, that it is a thriving place, that the existing accommodation is poor, I would be disposed to give careful consideration to a request of that kind. But if the people of another town came to me and, when asked as to whether there were already public buildings in another portion of the county, they answered in the affirmative, then, if the population was comparatively small. I would say:	You will have to wait for a
number of years until the population of! your town increases, and . you have three, or four thousand, or six thousand; then, you can fairly ask for a public building. In this particular case there is no other public building in the county.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the statement made by the Minister of Public Works because he has minutely described th/te condition of things in the county which I represent, in a matter that was brought to his notice a few evenings ago, I refer to the town of Milton. It is the shire town, it has a population of about 1,800, and, it is _ a thriving town. It has various industries, and there is no other public building in the whole county, no other building of any kind built by the government. It seems to _ me that every reason assigned bv the minister for the erection of a post office at Napierville, applies to the county town of my county with much greater force and I am delighted that the minister has given such strong assurances that when a case of that kind is made out, he will Mr. ARMSTRONG.
carefully consider it. The post office at Milton yields a large revenue, it is an industrial town, in the centre of a rich agricultural country, having everything in fact that^ would meet the requirements of the Minister of Public Works. I am simply drawing the minister's attention to this case, I am not asking him, as I told him the other night, I am not a beggar. I am not begging, but I am drawing this matter to his attention, so that when he reflects upon the course of his administration he will look to the town of Milton and say, There is a case where justice demands that something should be done. I am trying from time to time to make the mSnLs-1 ter's conscience feel as uncomfortable as possible. While I am not begging, I want to make him feel uncomfortably, becausej he has not done justice to this place.
